# Per-hack gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- Maze keeps a 1000 by 1000 maze and three 1,000,000-entry move lists in one
  `calloc` (about 20 MB; the board has 8 MB of PSRAM). `hacks/maze/maze.c`
  stays byte-identical: `firmware/patch_maze.py` (a PlatformIO `pre:` script
  in every env) writes a copy with both limits at 80 into the build dir, using
  `tools/maze_patch.py`, which fails loudly if upstream's `#define`s change.
  `hacks/maze_small.c` includes that copy and the original is excluded from
  `build_src_filter`. A `gridSize` below 7 would overflow the 80 by 80 arrays.
- Pacman has two build-time patches (`tools/pacman_patch.py`, run by
  `firmware/patch_pacman.py`; wrappers `hacks/pacman_stdlevel.c` and
  `hacks/pacman_loop_ai.c`): the random level generator recursed to ~315 KB
  and boot-looped the board, so a generated level is a copy from
  `hacks/pacman_pool.h` (24 levels, made on the host by
  `tools/pacman_levels.py` with the cells outside the round display walled
  off; the fixed level is still half of them), and the ghosts' route search is
  a loop (it was 453 levels deep). Re-run the tool after changing its mask or
  the generator's tile data. Each patch checks what it replaces. The two host
  pins that follow the game (`kBaseline`'s Pacman and the ghost-route chain)
  depend on how many `random()` values the level pick takes: re-take the chain
  with `pacman_loop_ai.c` temporarily including `pacman/pacman_ai.c`, then
  restore it and check the loop gives the same value. Its sprite sheet is
  built from `vendor/` into the build dir by `firmware/pacman_sprites.py` and
  never committed (3 MB as C text).
- Braid runs at 3-9 fps (0.8-2 before four rounds of work): it redraws every
  segment of the braid each frame to spin the colours. A host profile put its
  disc fill at 6% and the board spent most of its time there, because the Mac
  does `double` at full speed. Split a slow hack's step on the device with a
  temporary flag that returns early from the expensive call.
- Maze fills the whole 466 by 466 square, so its corners and the exit marker
  fall outside the round display's visible circle.
- `check_notices.py` reads 100 lines of header: Maze's licence follows a long
  modification history.
- A hack can be freed before its first draw: two quick presses, or a press
  with the 90 s rotation. `test_every_hack_can_be_stopped_before_its_first_frame`
  runs every hack through it. Blaster's free dereferenced NULL (it sizes a loop
  in init but allocates in draw), so `hacks/blaster_safe.c` includes the
  unmodified hack with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers it with a
  free that zeroes `NUM_ROBOTS` when `robots` is NULL.
- Deluxe is built through `hacks/deluxe_opaque.c`, which includes the unmodified
  hack with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers it with overrides:
  `*transparent: False` (upstream's plane masks need colour planes, which
  `allocate_alpha_colors` reports none of) and `*doubleBuffer: False` (it was
  added when the shim drew only on the canvas, so the `XCopyArea` from its
  blank pixmap erased the picture; pixmaps work now, but two 434 KB back
  buffers and a full-frame copy each frame would cost more than they give).
  The wrapper then gives each throbber's GC an alpha of 26
  of 32 (upstream's translucent weight) and sends full wide circles to
  `stroke_circle`. A plain screenhack's `HackEntry` has no overrides unless a
  wrapper builds it. Its step is 45-63 ms on the device against a 32.5 ms push,
  so about 11-13 fps (14 with 64-byte cache lines); overlapping the push with
  the next step (`repaints_all`) takes it to 19 fps. Other ideas are in issue
  #54.
- Eight of the S-hack batch (Anemone, Anemotaxis, Compass, FuzzyFlakes,
  Halftone, Interaggregate, LMorph, Wormhole) are built through
  `hacks/<name>_direct.c` (pixmap double buffering, see `techniques.md`;
  LMorph's is `lmorph_single.c` because it needs no `HAVE_JWXYZ`). All but
  Anemotaxis and Wormhole, and Euler2D (`euler2d_single.c`), also use
  `single_precision.h` plus build-time float literals (`patch_float_literals.py`
  lists them). `single_precision.h` leaves `floor` and `ceil` on the double
  versions: Euler2D's wrapper maps them itself. After the literal pass the
  objects still showed soft-double helpers: Interaggregate's were `frand` in
  `build_field` (fixed with `single_frand.h`); Halftone's, Anemone's and
  Euler2D's are in `*_init` only, once a start. `tools/softdouble_report.py`
  lists them by function.
- To see which hacks are worth a look, flash a build with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=20`,
  log the serial port for one lap (about 40 minutes), and run
  `uv run tools/triage_hacks.py lap.log --soft` (after `pio run -e stopwatch`).
  It sorts each hack into step-bound, push-bound or paced (its own delay is the
  biggest part of the frame) and puts the soft-double calls in its object
  beside it. A hack that is step-bound with calls is a wrapper candidate;
  step-bound with none is in its drawing, not its maths (Braid, Marbling,
  Discrete, BinaryRing); paced ones gain only what the step saves, down to the
  delay (Forest 500 ms, Vines 200 ms). A wrapper that moves nothing is worth
  dropping: Bouboule built single stayed at 14.5 ms, because its cost is
  ellipse fills.
- `test_frames_of_every_hack_but_maze_match_main` stops at the first hash that
  differs, in registry order, so repinning several hacks takes one test run
  each (about 85 s), earliest first. A hack whose frames do not change under a
  wrapper (Compass and Halftone in single precision) keeps its hash.
- Anemone's step moved between 31 and 56 ms as its arms grew and shrank, so its
  fps was 11 to 15.5 whatever one 20 s window said. Upstream opens every frame
  by filling the whole window black, which is a full frame of PSRAM writes
  (229,000 pixels a frame on the host, the strokes only about 16,000 of them),
  so `anemone_direct.c` erases only where last frame's lines were
  (`span_erase.h`, each line's box grown by its round caps): 31,000 pixels, the
  same frames, and only those rows dirty. On the board, over one 20 s window
  per lap: 30.5 fps mean (worst 20.4), step 25.2 ms. Counting pixels and
  spans written a frame on the host (a temporary counter in `hspan`) is a
  quick way to see what a hack costs before the device does. Forest waits
  500 ms between trees by design (about 2 fps, and the push is 88 rows).
- A hack that unpacks pixel values itself (Substrate and Interaggregate, in
  their `point2rgb`) assumes ordinary RGB565, but the canvas holds the bytes
  swapped. Its wrapper swaps pixels where they cross `XAllocColor` and
  `XSetForeground`. Interaggregate shipped without this: its alpha blends
  mixed the wrong bit fields and drew rainbow noise instead of green and brown
  strokes. `test_interaggregate_blend` includes the wrapper to check one blend.
- `dump` never seeds `random()`, so a hack that picks a mode at start (Truchet,
  12 modes) shows the same one in every dump. To see others, build the hack
  alone (`probe_hacks.registry_source` and `shim_sources`) from a copy outside
  `vendor/`, with a `__attribute__((constructor))` that calls
  `srandom(atoi(getenv("SEED")))`. Cheaper: drop a temporary
  `src/hacks/zz_seed_tmp.c` with that constructor, guarded by `SEED` being set
  (`-e dump` builds every file under `src/`), run
  `SEED=n .pio/build/dump/program <index> <frames> out.raw`, and delete the
  file before running the tests. A device boot is deterministic too (Halo
  chose Ramp on five boots in a row), so a hack that picks a mode with
  `random()` always starts the same one: force another with a temporary
  `*mode:` override to measure it. Rotation reaches other modes because the
  random state differs by then.
- Hexadrop (`hexadrop_single.c`) runs at about 10 fps, under the 15 fps bar.
  Splitting its step on the device showed the maths and the edge walk cost
  0.1 ms and all the rest is canvas writes: about 860 KB of 16-bit stores
  into the PSRAM canvas a frame. Single precision, a float convex fill and
  two-pixel stores took it from 2.4 to 10.2 fps with pixel-identical frames.
  More needs a shared canvas change or rasterising in row bands.
- Halo (`halo_direct.c`, `halo_planes.h`, `halo_circles.h`) draws whole circles
  into 1-bit pixmaps and XORs two of them. Its pixmaps are packed bit planes
  (27 KB each), not colour pixmaps: 434 KB colour stand-ins made Seuss mode
  (three runs in four) 5-9 fps, because window-sized circles are millions of
  PSRAM writes, and a float circle fill alone changed nothing. A device boot
  is deterministic, so every boot picked Ramp mode and hid that: force
  `*colorMode: seuss` temporarily to measure the other mode. It overrides
  `*delay` to 10 ms (upstream asks for 100 ms), so the circles grow faster.
- StonerView's seven files are built as one unit by `stonerview_gl.c`.
  Upstream never frees its oscillator list ("how do we free this?"), so the
  wrapper frees it through the `next` links before upstream's release.
- XMatrix needs `matrix_glyphs.py` (a `pre:` script in every env), which
  converts four PNGs from `vendor/` into blobs in the build directory: they
  are never committed (1.5 MB of C text each for the large sheets). It
  registers through `xmatrix_direct.c` with `*trace: False`, which skips the
  typed "connecting" sequence it would open with (the rare "Knock, knock,
  Neo" event, `knockKnock`, is still on); `*matrixFont: small`
  gives 46 columns instead of 23. Its text modes read no text: the
  `textclient.h` stand-in never opens a source, and Xt timers never fire.
- Flurry is not ported. It draws 3,600 blended, textured quads a frame and
  needs `glAlphaFunc`, `glRectd`, `gluBuild2DMipmaps` and luminance-alpha
  textures, none in TinyGL here. With `gl_budget.py`'s per-vertex and
  per-pixel costs that is well under 1 fps (arithmetic, not a measurement:
  the tool cannot read a multi-file hack).
- Qix and Fireworkx both leaked on every stop, found by the restart leak test.
  Qix's `qix_free` skips each segment's `lines[i].p` array (about 48 KB per
  stop); Fireworkx below 24 bits never frees its own 565 image buffer (48 KB).
  Their wrappers (`qix_direct.c`, `fireworkx_single.c`) free the missing piece
  before calling upstream's free. LeakSanitizer does not run on macOS, but
  `MallocStackLogging=1 leaks --atExit -- .pio/build/dump/program <index> 0
  out.raw` names the allocating line in seconds (rebuild `-e dump` first: a
  `pio test` deletes the program).
- Starfish and Goop spent most of a frame in the shim's polygon fill (double
  maths per edge per row). `hacks/float_polygon.h` fills any even-odd polygon
  in float, optionally mixed in at an alpha in 32nds (all three colour
  channels with one multiply), and took Starfish from 8.5 to 19 fps. Goop draws
  straight onto the window (its `XCreatePixmap` is the window and the
  `XCopyArea` is skipped) and blends each blob in at the alpha upstream's jwxyz
  path uses. Its full-frame clear cost 15 ms, so `hacks/span_erase.h` erases
  only the bounding boxes the blobs filled last frame (pixel-identical frames):
  14.6-15.2 fps translucent. The shared `canvas_fill_polygon` is integer now
  (see `x11shim.md`; Hexadrop has its own convex float fill). Goop is built through
  `goop_direct.c` with `HAVE_JWXYZ`; the colour-plane path needs planes the
  canvas lacks.
- A wrapper that does `#define double float` must include any header with a
  `double` in a struct the shim's `.c` files also use BEFORE the define: the
  hack includes it again, the guard keeps the copy seen through the macro, and
  the two sides disagree on the layout. `spline.h` did this to Starfish and
  Goop: they drew garbage (flat colours) at 16-20 fps and their first pinned
  hashes were of it. Look at a frame after any change that is not
  pixel-identical by construction;
  `test_hacks_that_use_the_spline_draw_a_real_picture` now fails on a flat
  screen.
- Fireworkx renders at 1/`FIREWORKX_SCALE` of the width and height
  (`hacks/lowrez_put.h`: it is told the window is smaller and `XPutImage`
  draws each pixel as a square): 2.4 fps as copied, 11 at a scale of 3, 12.4 at
  4. Its glow, flash pass and 565 conversion are full-frame walks over PSRAM.
  Its header says "(GPL)" but the text is the standard permission notice.
  Everything it works in is in pixels, tuned for a window about 1024 wide: at
  152 pixels a burst filled the picture and the glow blur (energy kept, output
  doubled) saturated, so the screen was white. `tools/fireworkx_patch.py`
  (run before the float literal pass; the copy stays byte-identical) scales the
  spark speed, gravity, flash reach and velocity jitter by the render width
  over 1024, and the wrapper throws 120 sparks a shell instead of 500 and fires
  two of its four shells. 12.4-12.6 fps, with a dark background between
  bursts. The shell count cannot change (it is baked into the SSE layout), so
  the idle shells are given an endless life and no sparks.
- Loop asks for 100 ms between generations (8.7 fps with a 3.5-7 ms step); the
  registry overrides it to 50 ms. It also took `malloc(0)` returning NULL, which
  the board does and the host does not, for out of memory: square mode asks
  for a rectangle list for each of eight colour states, most empty, and it
  freed its cells and drew nothing more (a black screen at 18 fps, half the
  starts, never seen on the host). `loop_direct.c` asks for one byte, and a test
  swaps in an allocator that returns NULL for zero. Hypnowheel was dropped from
  the rotation after Rod saw it, twice (issue #73; its source, notices row and a
  `failed_ports.txt` entry stay). `hypnowheel_single_gl.c` registers it only
  with `-DHYPNOWHEEL_PROBE`, as the last entry, for measuring. A board profile
  showed about 275 ms of its 706 ms step was `double` trig in every vertex, not
  fill as first thought; single precision gives 2.2 fps. The rest is fill
  (about 334 ms): `-DHYPNOWHEEL_HALF` renders at half resolution
  (`glshim_set_render_scale`) for 4.0 fps, still too slow for Rod.
- CWaves (`cwaves_single.c`) fills 233 columns, each a 2 by 466 rectangle, so
  every store lands on a different cache line of the PSRAM canvas: after single
  precision took the step from 95 to 61 ms, 57 of those were the fills and 4
  the cosines. The picture depends on x alone, so the wrapper writes each
  full-height column into canvas row 0 and the draw wrapper copies that row
  down (frames identical to the unmodified hack): 16 ms, 20 fps. Any hack that
  paints thin full-height strips can do the same.
- A single-precision wrapper must watch for a hack that passes the address of
  one of its own `double` locals to a shim function (`rgb_to_hsv (..., &fgs,
  &fgv)` in Moire): the prototype still says `double *`, so the float local is
  written eight bytes and the frames come out as colour noise, with no
  compiler warning. `moire_single.c` defines an adapter before
  `single_precision.h` and maps the name to it. Compare the wrapper's frames
  with the unmodified hack's: they were all different here, and identical once
  the adapter was in. A hack with no decimal literals (Moire) must not be in
  `patch_float_literals.py`, which refuses a file without any.
- Moire and Cynosure are paced by their own delays (Moire draws a 20-row chunk
  every 50 ms and holds each picture 5 s; Cynosure waits 500 ms a frame, which
  is upstream's default), so their fps is low whatever the step is. Cynosure's
  `XCreateBitmapFromData`, which the scorer lists as a gap, is inside a
  `DO_STIPPLE` block that is never defined.
- Moire2 (`moire2_direct.c`, `moire2_planes.h`, built on Halo's planes) keeps
  its four depth-1 pixmaps as bit planes and adds an outline circle, an XOR
  rectangle, an OR/XOR/copy between planes (the GC's `function`, which the shim
  now remembers) and a faster expansion to the window. Upstream's free leaves
  its pixmaps to the X server, and the runner frees only the shim's own, so the
  wrapper frees the planes. The first version ran at 9.6 fps: the plane copy
  and the expansion were 26 and 27 ms, because 64-bit index maths is several
  instructions an operation on a 32-bit core and the expansion branched on
  every pixel. After clipping everything fits an int; a byte table of eight
  pixels written four bytes at a time did the rest (28 ms). The 50 ms delay is
  overridden to 10 ms: 12.6 fps became 16.2.
- Boing was dropped after Rod saw it (too slow, and plain on a small screen);
  its source, notices row and `boing_gl.c` stay, the wrapper out of the build
  filter. Its 208 scanlines are blended full-width lines and cost half its
  step: 5.0 fps with them, 8.3 without; the ball size barely matters (0.3
  saves 13 ms). HexTrail (`hextrail_single_gl.c`) draws
  every hexagon it has built, so its step climbs from about 19 ms to a ceiling
  and it restarts: use a mean over a cycle (150 s). The grid is `count * 2`
  squared, and a smaller count makes fewer, larger hexagons over the same area:
  mean 5.7 fps at upstream's 20, 9.1 at 10, 12.7 at 6 (registered,
  `-DHEXTRAIL_COUNT=<n>`). Rod found 12.7 too slow once the picture filled
  (under 10 fps). Single precision gave 13.0; skipping the depth clear it
  never needs (see `gl.md`) gave 15.3, worst window 10.8. The single-precision
  wrapper adapts `get_position` and `get_rotation`: the hack passes `double`
  locals' addresses, which a float rename would write eight bytes (as Moire).
- Celtic (`celtic_single.c`, issue #37) is registered after HexTrail and takes
  a median step of 32 ms against 832 as copied (`assessment_measured.md.in`).
  The wrapper is single precision (`rint` and `floor` mapped to float: the
  header maps only some libm calls) and frees the colour table that
  `celtic_init` callocs. `tools/celtic_patch.py` does three things at build
  time. It works `t*n - floor(t*n)` out once and clamps it: in float a fused
  multiply-add made it slightly negative and the hack's `assert()` aborted
  (the 3000-frame test found it). It sizes the graph to the screen: upstream's
  margins of -600 to -900 left most of a pattern off the screen, one held 1.1
  MB on the host, and 44 of 300 random starts needed more than the board's free
  heap by a model; grid and Kennicott now use minus one edge, and the triangle
  width/2 plus two edges (its incircle is half its circumradius). And it
  scales the 0.0001 animation tick by `CELTIC_STEP_SCALE` (default 4,
  `-DCELTIC_STEP_SCALE=<n>`), which cuts the shadow look-ahead's work and a
  picture's draw calls to 100 / scale. A test bounds a pattern's host bytes
  over 150 starts. Do not shorten `*delay2`: it is a 5 s dwell on the finished
  picture upstream. It looked like a pause on black while the shim's
  `erase_window` cleared first (issue #86); now the first call leaves the
  picture up and the wipe follows the wait. When forcing a graph type in a
  scratch copy to compare, set the margin for that type too, or the triangle
  comes out too small to fill the screen.
- A full-frame write to the PSRAM canvas costs about 25 ms whatever does it
  (memcpy, a 2 by 2 blow-up, 32-bit stores). Eruption at half size
  (`eruption_direct.c`, `lowrez_put.h`, `-DERUPTION_SCALE`) spent 26 ms of a
  39 ms step putting its image and 13 ms on the fire. `lowrez_put.h` wants
  ordinary RGB565, so Eruption's palette is swapped at `XAllocColor`.
  Interference changes every pixel each frame; telling it the window is half
  the size changes its look (its wave table is in window pixels), so it stays
  at 10.2 fps.
- Kumppa rotates its picture with `XCopyArea` from the window onto itself.
  The fine checkerboard in its trails is the hack's: copies are checked
  against a read-everything-first reference in every overlap direction.
- Piecewise (`piecewise_direct.c`) is single precision with `single_frand.h`

  its random colour walk down, so every colour drifted to black or a dim
  green (as in BinaryRing). Pixels go straight to the window, and its image
  and pixmap are one pixel big, because nothing reads them. Every 30 s it

  that primitive: lines and fills still copy). `pow2.h` is our own

  its single-precision wrapper has an adapter (as Moire's). The restart test

- Bouboule's upstream default is a red and a blue starfield for 3D glasses,

  clip at the round bezel; `*tileSize` is the lever.

  also handle the hack's timed reload, which the shim finishes at once too, so
  upstream's "just finished" branch never runs again. It must also match image
  layouts: `XGetImage` gives a 32-bit image, and a hack that memcpys it into
  its own 16-bit buffer shows alternating black pixels. RotZoomer did on the
  board until the trail review caught it. Test with a flat grab image and
  assert every pixel, then change the image before a timed restart.

  frees its buffer) reads the clock separately from upstream, and the two reads
  can straddle a second. Read it once a frame and route upstream's `time()` to
  that reading with a function-like `#define time(p)`; test it with a fake
  clock whose second read is later.
- A hack that leaks on every in-hack restart (Munch's `get_string_resource`
  result) needs a restart-loop leak test of its own: `test_hacks` restarts only

  45.06 vs 45.12 ms, pinned, 2 rounds). Skip it; the step is the blend, the

  and one extra step pixmap: the wrapper frees both, and the leak test fails

  wrapper's `glColor4fv` scales its colour (the first frame is black, where

  draws them. Upstream wraps its palette index with `>` instead of `>=`, so

  Kaleidocycle also blends but its faces are opaque, so it was not folded.
- Kaleidocycle starts with `count = 0`, so its first frame computes a piece's
  angle as 0 / 0: a NaN that reaches TinyGL's viewport conversion and is cast to
  an int (the trail review found it with `-fsanitize=float-cast-overflow`:

  includes the build's patched copy (`generated/kaleidocycle_patched.c`, written

  wrapper premultiplies the texture as it uploads and has `glColor4f` scale its

  wave position.

  spinner glyph gets 1.5 times its brightness, and TinyGL masks a channel past
  full instead of saturating it, so a reproduced alpha of 1.087 gave green 5/63

  could not see it (a handful of pixels), so the helper is a plain header.

  signed `int`, which overflows for an alpha of 128 or more (a sanitizer sweep

  hexagons, so it needs no `glBegin` wrapper, and a test counts pure-red pixels
  over a run (3,166 at most; nothing else it draws is pure red). The first
  host run aborted in the 3,000-frame test on two over-reads (see `gl.md`).

  every stop leaked them: the wrapper frees them (payload, a diode's band, the
  component) before upstream's free, and the leak test fails without it. At
  full size on the board, over 240 s pinned: 8.4-11.4 fps (mean 9.7), step
  60-93 ms growing as components arrive, push 24.8 ms (every frame is a
  full push: the grid fills the screen), no wait, PSRAM flat. `gl_budget.py`
  predicted 79-85 ms a frame (12 fps) against about 103 measured (step plus
  push). It counts lines as free, and they are not (below).
  A single-precision build (ARS-55, committed and reverted: `b32fe24`,
  `bc549b2`) took `tools/softdouble_report.py`'s count in the wrapper's object
  from 198 call sites to 14 (the hack has no `double` keyword; its literals,
  `0.02` and `0.84`, were the cause) with host frames byte-identical, and moved
  the board by nothing: double and float alternated over two rounds, 28
  windows each, 9.76 vs 9.79 fps and a 77.6 vs 77.3 ms step. A `-DGL_PROFILE`

  board's grid (0.256 ms a line, every frame), 15.0 ms is the full-screen
  clear (the grid fills the box), about 18 ms is vertex setup, lighting,
  triangles and fills (growing from 1 ms to 32 ms as components arrive), and
  the hack's own code is 6.3 ms: the most any arithmetic change could win is
  8 percent. The lever is the grid's lines, not Circuit's maths.
  `-DCIRCUIT_HALF` renders at half the width and height
  (`glshim_set_render_scale(2)`, as Menger does). Alternating it with full
  size on the board, two rounds each (about 57 windows a build): full 9.67
  fps (8.4-11.6, step 78.6 ms), half 14.78 fps (13.0-18.4, step 42.1 ms); the

  blocky against the fine grid lines (2-pixel lines, chunky resistor bands and
  display dot), so it is opt-in, not the default. It leaves 217 KB more PSRAM
  free (6,049,231 against 5,832,095; `psram=` is free memory, and an earlier
  note here said the opposite). A scale-2 hack cannot overlap its push, so the
  registry flags Circuit `repaints_all` only without `-DCIRCUIT_HALF`.
  The flag earned its place narrowly. Pinned, alternating with
  `-DPUSH_NO_OVERLAP`, two rounds each (about 57 windows a build): plain 9.50
  fps (step 80.5 ms, push 24.8 ms), overlapped 10.29 fps (step 97.2 ms, push
  0.1 ms), +8.3 percent; window by window the ratio averaged 1.08 (0.98 to

  contend for the PSRAM cache and Circuit's lines are miss-heavy (a cache
  simulation of its real line pixels gives about 33,000 misses a frame, 1.1

  milliseconds. It also takes 8.7 KB of internal heap.
  Line batching (see `gl.md`) then took the registered build from 10.59 to
  13.55 fps over two alternating rounds (step 93.2 to 72.3 ms, worst window
  9.2 to 11.6, best 16.2), with frames byte-identical. That is full size and
  crisp, but still under the 15 fps bar. The profile has not been taken again
  with batching on; before it, the clear was 15 ms and vertex setup, lighting
  and fills about 18 ms of the step.

# X11 shim and framework gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- `unsigned long` is 4 bytes on the device and 8 on the host, so a hack that
  allocates arrays of it (Substrate's two 466 by 466 buffers) is twice the size
  on the host, and host leak numbers are twice the device's. On the device,
  plain `malloc`/`realloc` of about 868 KB reached PSRAM (free PSRAM fell by
  1.74 MB) and came back on restart; internal heap barely moved.
- The board's `malloc` is `CONFIG_SPIRAM_USE_MALLOC=y` with
  `SPIRAM_MALLOC_ALWAYSINTERNAL=4096`: a block up to 4 KB comes from internal
  RAM and falls back to PSRAM when that is full, and a bigger one goes to PSRAM
  first. An allocation fails only when PSRAM is gone, so a hack's `abort()` on
  a failed allocation is not the risk it looks. The cost of a big pattern is
  internal heap drained to near zero (Celtic read 1,792 B free) and its data
  in slower PSRAM: compare the log's `psram=` with its idle value for the
  overflow.
- `erase_window` (`erase.c`) follows upstream's contract: the first call draws
  nothing and returns a state, so a hack that waits after it (Celtic's 5 s
  `*delay2`) waits on the finished picture. The second call starts a one-second
  wipe (blinds, circle, fizzle or random lines, picked at random), each later
  call draws the next step, and the call after the second is up clears the
  window and returns NULL. Progress comes from `double_time()`, not from the
  call count, so the wipe lasts a second at any step rate. A test or tool
  that does not sleep for a hack's delay must install a clock
  (`xshim_set_clock`), or a wipe never ends. Six hacks never call
  `eraser_free`, so the display tracks live states and the runner releases
  them when a hack stops.
- xlockmore hacks (the 40 that include `xlockmore.h`) need `-DSTANDALONE`,
  which every PlatformIO env and `score_hacks.py` set; without it they
  include `xlock.h` instead. The envs also define `HAVE_MOBILE`, because
  otherwise each hack's `XSCREENSAVER_LINK` defines the same global
  `xscreensaver_function_table` and two hacks fail to link; the only other
  effect is an inert `*ignoreRotation: True` default. Register one in
  `hacks/registry.c` with `XLOCKMORE_HACK(<name>, "<Class>")`. The runner runs
  the hack's `setup_cb` once and passes `setup_arg` as `init_cb`'s hidden third
  argument, as xscreensaver's `screenhack.c` does. Its table is empty until
  then. Resources the framework reads but a hack does not define
  (`delta3d`, `size`, ...) fall back to `kFrameworkDefaults` in
  `x11shim/resources.c`. A `HackEntry`'s `overrides` list beats the hack's own
  defaults (Galaxy runs with `count: -3`, at most three galaxies; a count of
  -2 or above skips the hack's restart cleanup and leaks); register it with
  `XLOCKMORE_HACK_WITH`. Galaxy, Drift, Discrete and Flame are built through
  `hacks/<name>_single.c`, which includes the framework headers, then
  `hacks/single_precision.h` (`double` and the libm calls become `float` and
  the `f` versions; the S3's FPU is single-precision only), then the unmodified
  hack; the original `.c` is excluded from each env's `build_src_filter`.
- Wide lines (`line_width` above 1), arcs and pixmap writes live in
  `x11shim/stroke.c`, `arc.c` and `pixmap.c`. Width 0 and 1 keep the old
  `canvas_line` path, so hacks that set no wide width are pixel-identical (every
  hack's frame is pinned in `test_hacks.c`). Braid is the one registered hack
  that draws wide lines (random width 1-7; Maze's width 2 is under
  `HAVE_JWXYZ`). A round-capped segment draws a disc at each end, so
  `stroke.c` keeps each width's rows in a table (widths to 16) rather than
  calling `canvas_fill_ellipse` (which used to do `double` maths per row, in
  software on the S3; see below). A test pins the pixels to
  `canvas_fill_ellipse`.
- `canvas_fill_ellipse` and `canvas_fill_polygon` work in whole numbers, not
  double (the S3 does double in software). The ellipse is exact: a pixel is in
  when `dx2^2 * h^2 <= w^2 * (h^2 - dy2^2)` with distances doubled, and a float
  `sqrt` only starts the search for each row (it is wrong by one at 220 by 21,
  264 by 23, 312 by 25 and 318 by 181, which the tests pin). The polygon steps
  each edge's crossing with a quotient and remainder, no division per row, and
  a pixel on a left edge is in and one on a right edge is out. The old double
  fill was not consistent at exact ties (a 45 degree edge through integer
  vertices): it left stray hatch marks on Qix's thin sliver polygons, so Qix
  (612 pixels) and Pedal (3) re-pinned. Sizes or coordinates past 32768 and
  2^24 keep the double code. On the board (step, before to after): Bouboule
  14.5 to 5.2 ms (27.4 to 36.8 fps), Qix 14.6 to 1.9 ms (37.3 to 70.1 fps),
  Pedal 21.8 to 8.6 ms (it then holds the picture for 5 s).
- A circle (`w == h`, up to 32) keeps its rows in a table by diameter, relative
  to its corner: the centre column is `2x + w - 1` and `floor_half(2x + k)` is
  `x + floor_half(k)`, so the rows do not depend on where it sits. Integer
  rows alone took Halftone (about 1,150 dots a frame) from 5 to 9.8 fps, push
  overlap to 11.4-12.0, and the table to 14.2-14.6 (#57). The row-clip bounds
  in `fill_cached_circle` are speed guards only, since `hspan` clips: removing
  them is an equivalent mutant, as is reversing the rows (a circle is symmetric).
- Lisa was the counter-example to "the stroker maths is the cost" (#98), and
  then the maths turned out to be the cost after all. Converting a slanted
  segment's ends from int to float moved it by nothing (52.1 ms either way),
  and with the line calls compiled out its step is 5.2 ms, so 47 ms of 52 was
  drawing: 1,396 segments and 6.7k spans a frame at width 2, 13k spans at
  width 8. The guess was a PSRAM cache miss per scattered span. The real
  cost was `fill_convex`: the S3 has no float divide, min, max, floor or
  64-bit conversion, so its per-row loop (two divides, `fminf`, `fmaxf`, two
  `floorf` and two `__fixsfdi` calls a row) was about 3 us a span. It now
  divides each edge's slope once per polygon and uses compares and 32-bit
  `floor_int`. That rounds a few ulps differently from dividing first, which
  moved pixels on a boundary (review of #128): a row whose span ends are within
  rounding of a boundary decision is worked out the old way, and the pixels
  match main's. Test it with each stroke on a cleared canvas
  (`test_wide_strokes_of_random_lines_match_the_pinned_hash`, pinned from main's
  rasteriser): a hash of strokes drawn together missed it, because later strokes
  covered the pixels that differed. Checking every edge of every row cost most
  of the gain (Lisa 43 ms at width 2); checking the two span ends and reusing
  their floors keeps it. On the board Lisa's step went 52.3 to 38.5 ms at width
  2 (14.2 to 17.7 fps) and 85.4 to 60.1 ms at width 8 (9.7 to 12.9 fps), Braid
  125.4 to about 94 ms (8.1 to 9.7 fps) and Deluxe 51.9 to 49.2 ms (19.0 to
  19.9 fps), two rounds each. The width
  sweep on the host (`-DLW=N` with `LINEWIDTH` edited, temporarily) shows the
  cliff is thin to wide: width 1 takes the `canvas_line` path at 0.09 ms, width
  2 is 0.52 ms and width 8 0.85 ms. Look for the same library calls in a
  per-row or per-pixel loop of any hack: `nm` on the object lists them
  (`__divsf3`, `__fixsfdi`, `floorf`, `sqrtf`).
- `canvas_line` (thin lines, width 0 and 1) keeps its endpoints as ints when
  nothing is clipped: it used to convert all four to double and back, which
  the S3 does in software, on every call. Pixels are
  unchanged (`test_lines_inside_the_canvas_match_the_reference` and the
  off-canvas twin draw 20,000 lines each, alone, with `canvas_line` and with a
  copy of the old one in the test file). Compare against a reference copy, not
  a pinned hash, for anything that goes through `clip_line`: its double
  arithmetic rounds differently when the compiler contracts to FMA, and a hash
  taken on one setting fails on the other. On the board XRaySwarm's step went
  21.05 to 13.20 ms (23.2 to 28.3 fps; about 9,700 short lines a step);
  Wormhole 26.9 to 26.0 ms and NerveRot 48.2 to 46.7 ms barely move, since
  they draw far fewer lines and clip some.
  Counting calls on the host (a scratch copy with counters in `canvas_line`,
  `arc_points`, `compute_closed_spline`) put 29 of 109 hacks on `canvas_line`.
  The colour-map builders in `helpers.c` run at start only, so their double
  maths does not matter per frame.
- `canvas_line`'s clip (`clip_line_integer`, `canvas.c`) is the Liang-Barsky
  clip in exact `int64` rationals: it compares the quotients by
  cross-multiplying and rounds each end with one integer divide. The double
  clip (`clip_line`) still decides two cases, and `canvas_line` falls back to
  it for them: an end exactly on a half pixel, where double rounding can land
  either side, and a coordinate past 2^20. The limit comes from an error bound
  (double's error stays near 1e-10, while a rational answer that is not
  exactly on a boundary is at least 1 / 2^22 from it), not from a test: a
  raised limit survives the random tests, since a miss at 10^9 is about one
  in ten million lines. A clipped end sits on the canvas border, so one
  coordinate is an integer and only the other can tie. Pixels match the old
  clip in every reference test, with FMA contraction on and off (a mutant that
  treats every integer as a tie falls back every time and so also passes). On
  the board XSpirograph's step went 11.4 to 7.45 ms (15.2 to 16.8 fps: its
  push, 18.3 to 16.3 ms, now sets the frame) with 404 of 722 lines a step
  clipped; Laser 21.3 to 20.8 ms (52% clipped, but about 270 pixels a line);
  Deco unchanged at 34.3 ms (its own delay holds it at 0.2 fps).
- `arc_points` (`arc.c`) and `compute_closed_spline` (`spline.c`) take a fast
  path and keep the old arithmetic for what the fast path cannot settle. Both
  match the old code point for point in the reference tests, with FMA
  contraction on and off; the pinned frame of every hack is unchanged.
  - `compute_closed_spline` works each point's blend of four controls in
    float (the weights are worked out once, in double, then kept as float) and
    keeps it unless it is within about 1e-3 plus 2e-6 of the largest control
    from a half pixel, where `lround` could go either way; then the original
    double expression decides. Controls past 1e6 in size take the double path
    throughout. The controls are `double` because hacks fill them in, so the
    conversion to float is once a call, not once a point. Goop: step 45.3 to
    35.4 ms (15.9 to 18.9 fps), about 500 points a step.
  - `arc_points` works a run of 16 points from the first by rotating through
    the step between points (four multiplies and two adds, not a divide, `sinf`
    and `cosf`), and a point within 2e-3 plus 4e-5 of the radius from a rounding
    boundary is worked out as before, and the rotation reseeded from it. Angles
    past 32 radians (float's spacing is then near a millionth of a radian) and
    coordinates or radii past 1e6 take the plain loop. The run length is a
    margin: the real drift over a thousand points is about 1e-3 px against a
    tolerance of 0.02 px, so a longer run passes the tests too. Piecewise:
    step 43.4 to 38.6 ms (22.4 to 25.0 fps, about 3,200 arc points a step);
    BoxFit 14.1 to 12.9 ms, with its fps flat (19.1 to 19.2) because its own
    delay sets the frame.
  - A mutant that drops the near-half fallback, one that flips a rotation
    sign, and ones that remove the angle or coordinate limits are each killed
    by the reference tests; a pinned hash would not do here either, since the
    float and double paths can round a half pixel differently.
- `single_precision.h` renames the keyword `double`, not literals: `0.5 * x`
  is still software double. Braid's wrapper includes a copy of the hack with
  every decimal literal suffixed `f`, written at build time by
  `firmware/patch_float_literals.py` (`tools/float_literals.py`). Check a
  wrapper's object for `__muldf3` and friends with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm`.
  `uv run tools/softdouble_report.py <name>` does that for every object in
  the device build, by function: a count in a per-frame function is a literal
  or a macro the header could not reach. It lists none in Galaxy, Discrete,
  Drift, Flame, Substrate or Interaggregate now.
- Four things hide soft double from `single_precision.h`, each found by that
  report. `frand` (`single_frand.h`) and `MAXRAND`, `M_PI`, `M_PI_2` and
  `M_PI_4` (`single_constants.h`) are macros with a decimal literal in their
  body, past the literal pass; both headers are opt-in, since each moves the
  wrapper's frames and pins. Exponent literals (`1e-6`, `1.0E5`) were skipped
  by `float_literals.py` until Drift and Flame showed one each. A struct
  declared with `double` fields before the rename keeps them, so a float
  `corners[j].x * size` plus a `double` `pos.x` is a software add: HexTrail's
  `XYZ` (from `normals.h`) was 94 calls in `draw_hextrail`. Give the hack its
  own float struct under the same name, and `normals.h` another name for the
  double one (`hextrail_single_gl.c`; frames byte-identical). And a trig
  argument that is a big whole number cannot be a float: XSpirograph's second
  angle is millions of degrees and Vines' is an `int` in the billions, so a
  plain `double` to `float` turned both pictures to noise. XSpirograph reduces
  its angles mod 360 in integers at build time (`tools/xspirograph_patch.py`);
  Vines builds `(double) a` as `(long) a`, so its `cos` macro gets the exact
  integer and takes the phase as a 64-bit multiply by 2^64 / 2 pi, wrapping
  into whole turns (`vines_single.c`). Look at a frame before trusting a
  float build of anything whose angles grow. To find the line of a stray
  promotion, add `-Wdouble-promotion -fsyntax-only` to a file's compile
  command in `firmware/compile_commands.json` (`pio run -e stopwatch -t
  compiledb`; delete the file afterwards, it upsets the editor).
- A colour pixmap is a `Canvas`, and every drawing primitive draws on the
  drawable it is given (`xshim_target` in `pixmap.c`); `None` draws nothing,
  and a bitmap takes only `XCopyArea`, `XCopyPlane` and filled rectangles and
  polygons (see below). One exception still draws on the window whatever
  it is given: Deluxe's wrapper, which calls `stroke_circle(dpy->canvas,
  ...)`. No
  registered hack drew into a pixmap before this (the `HAVE_JWXYZ` wrappers
  and Deluxe's `doubleBuffer: False` turn double-buffering off), so keep
  those: a back buffer costs 434 KB and a full-frame copy, and dirties every
  row. Without a
  clip mask, `XCopyArea` copies colour rows whole with `canvas_paste_rect`. A
  pixmap wider or taller than `INT16_MAX` is `None` (the canvas's dirty spans
  are `int16_t`). Truchet draws into one (issue #61). The display tracks every
  pixmap a hack holds and the runner frees what a stopped hack left behind
  (Pacman leaked 514 KB per start). The GC keeps its own copy of a clip mask
  because hacks free the pixmap right after `XSetClipMask`. There is no PNG
  decoder: `image_data_to_pixmap` reads
  the raw blob described in `ximage-loader.h`, made by
  `tools/make_logo_blob.py` (`uv run`, needs Pillow). Pacman's sprites,
  XMatrix's large glyph sheets and the grab image are built with `--deflate`
  ("565Z", issue #102): 1.39 MB of flash saved, unpacked into a temporary
  buffer while the image loads (Pacman's is 522 KB of PSRAM, briefly), by the
  ROM's `tinfl` on the device and zlib on the host, so host builds link `-lz`
  (`platformio.ini`, `probe_hacks.py`, `gl_budget.py`). Host tests cover only
  zlib. XMatrix's small sheets are never drawn at 466 px: their generated
  headers `#define` them to the large ones. The `logo_180`/`360`
  headers are aliases of the 50 px data, as a 466 px screen only picks 50.
  `XS_LOGO=<image>` (relative to the repo root) swaps the logo for a local
  image, shrunk to fit 50 px, without committing it: `firmware/logo_override.py`
  writes the header into the build dir, where `maze_patched.c` finds it
  before the committed one. Unset, it deletes that header. Needs `uv`. A
  third-party logo kept under `vendor/` stays out of git that way. The WorkOS
  icon is `vendor/workos/workos-icon-256.png`. A plain flash with it is
  `unset PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` then `XS_LOGO=vendor/workos/workos-icon-256.png
  pio run -e stopwatch -t upload`: build flags stick, so a leftover pin from
  an earlier probe would survive. The logo shows in Maze only.
- A wide circle through `XDrawArc` is a polyline of about a thousand wide
  segments, each filled a row at a time: 40 times the fills of a ring, and the
  polyline leaves gaps in it. `stroke_circle` (`x11shim/stroke.c`) fills the
  ring in two spans a row. Only Deluxe's wrapper calls it, and it does full
  circles only: Pacman's wall arcs are quarters and Celtic's wide strokes are
  lines, so they still take the stroker. The polyline's gaps were float
  rounding, not the joins or the point spacing: a pixel centre exactly on an
  edge shared by a segment quad and the join wedge at its end (any 45 degree
  edge through integer vertices) fell out of both, because float32 put the
  quad's right edge at 57.499996 for 57.5. `fill_convex` now takes a right
  edge inclusive to within `EDGE_SLACK` (1e-3; 1e-7 fails the test, 1e-5
  passes), and `test_wide_full_arc_fills_every_pixel_in_its_band` pins it. It
  moved five pinned frames by 0 to 33 pixels each (Deluxe, Forest, Rotor,
  Compass, Celtic). Pacman is not affected: its `wallwidth` is 1 at this
  size, which takes the thin-line path. Celtic's overpaint (about 50 paints a
  pixel a step on the host, 46% of its line draws zero-length) is still open
  in #56. Changing shared stroke code can move pinned frames: look at them and
  ask Rod. The pin test hashes steps 50, 100, 150 and 200 with a fake clock
  that carries across hacks, so a dump program does not reproduce its frames:
  write them from the test itself.
- `XshimGC.alpha` (0 is opaque, 1 to 31 is the weight out of 32) makes the
  wide-line code in `stroke.c` blend over the canvas instead of overwriting it;
  fills, `canvas_line` and the other primitives ignore it. The canvas is
  byte-swapped RGB565, so the blend swaps each pixel and back. A shape of
  overlapping pieces (a polyline, a round cap and its segment) sets bits in a
  mask the size of the canvas (a 27 KB `calloc` per shape, freed at the end)
  and blends it once, or the overlaps blend twice and a star's corners show
  as bright diamonds. A failed `calloc` falls back to blending piece by piece.
  Setting `alpha` takes a wrapper, as in `hacks/deluxe_opaque.c`.
- Don't declare `xrealloc` or `xmalloc` in the shim: cloudlife defines its own
  static `xrealloc`, which would clash.
- `XGetImage` and `XPutImage` (`ximage.c`) move 32-bit ZPixmap images (the raw
  RGB565 value in each) to and from the window or a colour pixmap; a bitmap
  format, `None` or an empty region gives NULL. XMatrix flips its glyph sheets
  through them. Overrunning a row's right edge wraps onto the next row without
  AddressSanitizer seeing it, so a clip test must look at that next row.
- `XPutImage` copies a 16-bit image a row at a time with `memcpy`; other
  depths keep the per-pixel loop, since they keep only the low 16 bits (#82).
  ad-flyingtoasters at 2x: step 29.3 to 6.7 ms, 22.3 to 28.5 fps; at 1x: step
  15.9 to 3.7 ms. Fireworkx draws its own squares and did not change.
- `image_data_to_pixmap` accepts a NULL width, height or mask pointer (XMatrix
  passes no mask, and a NULL mask used to crash it on start); with no mask
  pointer no mask is made.
- `XClearWindow` clears to the colour `XSetWindowBackground` last set
  (default 0), and `xshim_release_pixmaps` resets it when a hack stops: the
  display outlives the hack, and Hexadrop's colour once turned Pyro's clear
  into a solid fill. No key events ever arrive, so `XLookupString` finds no
  characters, and an Xt timer (`X11/Intrinsic.h`) is never made.
- The shim still draws nothing into a depth-1 pixmap and draws every GC as
  `GXcopy`; it only remembers the function in `gc->function` now (GXcopy, GXor,
  GXxor). Halo and Moire2 handle both inside their own wrappers
  (`halo_planes.h`, `moire2_planes.h`).
- `screenhack.h`'s `frand` has a `1.0` inside its macro body, so the float
  literal pass cannot reach it and a single-precision wrapper still divides in
  double (software on the S3; `nm` shows `__divdf3`). `hacks/single_frand.h`
  redefines it in float; it is opt-in, because the older wrappers' frame hashes
  are pinned with the original.
- Added for the second batch, each test-first: 16-bit ZPixmap `XImage`s
  (canvas-order pixels, like every other value the shim hands out: `XAllocColor`
  -> `XPutPixel` -> `XPutImage` keeps the pixel; `XPutImage` does not swap.
  Only `lowrez_put_image` swaps, because Fireworkx writes ordinary RGB565
  bytes straight into the image data) and
  `ImageByteOrder`; `CoordModePrevious` in `XFillPolygon`, `XDrawLines` and
  `XDrawPoints`; `XCreatePixmapFromBitmapData` (X bitmap data is least
  significant bit first); a spline of our own (`spline.c`, not xscreensaver's);
  `XQueryColor`; `DisplayOfScreen` (the display opened last); the fill-rule,
  fill-style and stipple constants (accepted, ignored: fills are solid and
  even-odd); and `XSetFunction` and `jwxyz_XSetAlphaAllowed` (no-ops).
- Added for the third batch, each test-first: `ya_random` (the C library's
  `random()`, so `ya_rand_init` seeds it); `make_color_ramp` (the short way
  round the hue wheel, there and back when `closed_p`; ours, not
  xscreensaver's); `visual_depth` (always 16); `xshm.h` with
  `create_xshm_image`, `put_xshm_image` and `destroy_xshm_image`, which are a
  zeroed 16-bit `XImage` and `XPutImage` (`x11shim/xshm.c`); the arrow and page
  keysym constants (X's values; no key event ever arrives); and `glOrtho` (see
  `gl.md`). The Edit tool drops a trailing space from `old_string` and
  `new_string`: an edit that ends at a space in `platformio.ini`'s
  `build_src_filter` glued two entries together (it still built, which hid it).
- `allocate_alpha_colors` still finds no colour planes, so a hack that wants
  transparency (Qix, Goop) falls back to opaque layers and prints "couldn't
  allocate any color planes" on the host.
- The comment in `xshim.h` saying `XPutImage` byte-swaps a 16-bit image has
  been stale since commit 272ad6a: an `XImage` holds canvas-order pixels. A
  hack that builds its own 16-bit image must `px_swap` its pixels first.
- Added for the 2026-10-12 batch, each test-first: `XCopyArea` from the
  window (onto itself, rows moved with `memmove` in the order that reads each
  first, or into a pixmap); `XSetGraphicsExposures`; `make_color_loop` (ours);
  `grabclient.h` with `load_image_async_simple`, which finishes at once, with
  the grab image painted if one is set (below); `thread_util.h`, a pool that
  runs each thread in turn on the caller, as upstream does without pthreads;
  `visual_pixmap_depth`; `XCharStruct`; and `image_data_to_ximage` (RGBA
  bytes, bottom row first). `screenhack.h` now includes `visual.h` and
  `grabclient.h`, as upstream's does.
- `tools/wire_hack.py` puts a new hack before the After Dark toasters'
  `#ifdef` in the registry, the expected list and `kBaseline`.
- Added for the 2026-10-12 second batch, each test-first: `XClearArea` (the
  window background, clipped; a width or height of 0 runs to the window's
  edge; Worm), `XMaxRequestSize` (65535, so Lisa batches about 32,000 points a
  call) and the `LineOnOffDash` and `LineDoubleDash` constants (accepted;
  lines still draw solid; Penrose uses them only in its monochrome path). The
  scorer's gap list was wrong for Triangle (`free_colors` and
  `make_smooth_colormap` exist; its xlockmore include chain just does not
  reach `colors.h`, so `hacks/triangle_colors.c` includes `screenhack.h`

  `HAVE_GETTIMEOFDAY`, which upstream takes from `config.h`:

  `screenhackI.h` would have fixed Triangle for all but changes what every
  xlockmore hack sees, so it is Rod's call.
- `XFillRectangle` and `XFillPolygon` fill a depth-1 pixmap now (Rocks): a bit
  is set where the GC's foreground is odd and cleared where it is even, and the
  clip mask and the GC's function are ignored. The polygon is even-odd, a pixel
  being in when its centre is, in float. Other primitives still draw nothing on
  a bitmap. Halo, Moire2 and Goop keep their own planes or layers and did not
  move.
- `xshim_set_grab_image` (`grabclient.h`) gives `load_image_async_simple` a
  picture to paint over its target the next time a load starts: scaled to cover
  and cropped evenly at the sides (a 4:3 screenshot on the square screen loses
  its left and right edges), mask ignored, finishing at once as before. `main.cpp`
  sets it from the header `firmware/grab_image.py` writes into the build
  directory: `firmware/assets/grab-image.png` (Rod's choice: the Windows 95
  screenshot from guidebookgallery.org, committed at his say-so, with a
  notices section), or `XS_GRAB_IMAGE=<file>`, and `XS_GRAB_IMAGE=none` builds
  without. It is stored at up to 466 pixels (a 466 by 350 blob was 340
  KB of flash, 48 KB since it was deflated in #102: the build had gone from
  2.39 MB to 2.74 MB, 87.0% of the app partition). The host tests set their
  own picture, so a pin never depends on the local file; `dump` sets it when
  the header exists. DecayScreen is unpinned for that reason
  (`test_decayscreen_melts_the_grab_image`). Boxfit's `grab` mode, off by
  default, would get the picture too.
- `make_smooth_colormap` follows upstream's behaviour (written from scratch, not
  copied): two to five random points in hue, saturation and value, repicked if
  adjacent ones are close or the average is too grey or dark, joined in a closed
  path with colours spaced by edge length. The first version always spanned the
  hue wheel at high saturation and value, so Triangle and 23 other pinned hacks
  were a bright rainbow.
- The Xft stand-in (`xft.h`, `xft.c`, `xft_font.h`; ours) draws 8-bit coverage
  glyphs, blended over the canvas pixel by pixel (the canvas is byte-swapped
  565, so each pixel is swapped, weighed in 8-bit channels and packed again),
  clipped in 64 bits and marked dirty once a glyph. It ignores the GC's clip
  mask, as Xft does. The glyph data is baked from `assets/fonts/` at 12, 16,

content.text:
Rod, Phosphor is doable but not small. I stopped at the scoping stage and haven't written any code. The port is an L-rated job, but L here comes from one cluster of 1-bit bitmap gaps, not from a pile of missing calls.

**What I found**
- **Already in the shim:**
  - `textclient.h`, `X11/Intrinsic.h` and the Xft stand-in all exist.
  - Cursor blink won't run, because Xt timers never fire. The cursor just stays on.
- **Copy as-is:** `ansi-tty.c` and `ansi-tty.h` have the standard jwz licence, so they need a notices row.
- **Shim gaps to fill, test-first:**
  - `blurb.h`.
  - `utf8_encode` and `utf8_decode`, which `ansi-tty.c` uses.
  - A "565Z" blob of `6x10font.png`, committed as a small generated header like the logos.
- **The hard part is the glyph pipeline:** it assumes real 1-bit pixmaps. The shim can't `XDrawLine` into a bitmap, `XGetImage` a bitmap, or `XPutImage` onto one.
- **My plan for that:** a `phosphor_*.c` wrapper that leaves `phosphor.c` byte-identical. It replaces `capture_font_bits` with a version built from `image_data_to_ximage`, and routes `XDrawLine` on a bitmap to a rectangle fill. That keeps the change out of the shared shim.
- **Settings I'd change:**
  - The default scale of 6 gives only a 12×7 grid on 466 px, so I'd override it to about 3 (roughly 25×15).
  - `cache` must be off. At that scale the per-glyph fade cache is around 20 MB, against 8 MB of PSRAM.
- **Text source:** with no pty on the board, the wrapper needs its own `textclient`. It would be a short canned, deterministic terminal session using a few ANSI sequences, which also makes it testable. The shared `textclient.h` stays as it is, so XMatrix is untouched.
- **Open risk:** the speed. Every fading cell is redrawn every frame, so I'd expect a few hundred cell redraws a frame. I won't know the fps until it runs.

**Two things I need from you**
1. There's no Linear ticket for Phosphor (I searched the ARS team). AGENTS.md says to ask before working untracked: shall I file one?
2. Are you happy with the wrapper approach? It leaves the shared shim and `textclient.h` alone, but it means a canned text session instead of real `xscreensaver-text` output.

I'm on branch `wip/phosphor-port` with nothing changed. Once you've answered, I'll start with the failing registry test.

# Linear tracking

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

## Filing issues

- Every issue gets the `stopwatch-screensaver` label (in the `Repo` group) and exactly
  one label from the `Work Type` group. The group is single-select, so
  pick the one that fits best (see below).
- Always set a priority (Urgent, High, Medium, Low). Never leave it at
  "No priority".
- Link the draft trail or spec section if one exists. Copy the body from
  `entire trail show N --json`; `entire trail list --json` returns empty
  bodies.

## Choosing a Work Type

| Label         | Use it for                                       |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `Bug`         | Fixing something that isn't operating correctly. |
| `Feature`     | Adding new functionality to the app.             |
| `Enhancement` | Improving existing functionality.                |
| `Performance` | Improving the performance of code.               |
| `Chore`       | Maintenance, tooling and documentation work.     |

Several of these can fit one ticket. Decide by asking these in order and
taking the first yes:

1. Does the app do something other than what was intended? `Bug`, even if
   the symptom is slowness or the fix is a refactor.
1. Is the behaviour right, but too slow or heavy, and is speed or
   resource use the point of the work? `Performance`.
1. Does it give the user a capability they did not have? `Feature`.
1. Does it make a capability they already have better? `Enhancement`.
1. Does it change nothing a user would notice? `Chore`.

A ticket that bundles small, unrelated tidy-ups takes `Chore`. If the
bundle is mostly one other type, either split it or use that type.
Refactors, test additions, dependency bumps, build scripts, CI and
documentation are `Chore` unless they fix a defect.

## Status names

Use these exactly as Linear spells them: `Backlog`, `Todo`,
`In Progress`, `In Review`, `Done`, `Canceled`, `Duplicate`.

GUARD = "#ifdef HAVE_AFTER_DARK_TOASTERS\n"


def _guard_in(text: str, start: str, end: str) -> int:
    """Index of GUARD between `start` and `end`, or -1."""
    a = text.find(start)
    b = text.find(end, a)
    if a < 0 or b < 0:
        return -1
    return text.find(GUARD, a, b)


def wire(
    root: Path,
    name: str,
    cls: str,
    copyright_text: str,
    notice: str = "jwz permission notice (above)",
    xlockmore: bool = False,
    glx: bool = False,
) -> None:
    src = root / UPSTREAM / "hacks" / ("glx" if glx else "") / f"{name}.c"
    if not src.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(src)
    dst = root / "firmware" / "src" / "hacks" / name / f"{name}.c"
    registry = root / "firmware" / "src" / "hacks" / "registry.c"
    tests = root / "firmware" / "test" / "test_hacks" / "test_hacks.c"
    notices = root / "THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md"

    reg = registry.read_text()
    if re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(name)}_hack\b", reg):
        raise ValueError(f"{name} is already in registry.c")
    if xlockmore:
        decl = f'XLOCKMORE_HACK({name}, "{cls}");\n'
    else:

### The Maze logo

Maze draws the xscreensaver logo inside its maze. The logo data in
`logo-50_png.h` is `utils/images/logo-50.gif` from xscreensaver 6.17,
re-encoded as 50 by 50 RGB565 pixels and a transparency mask, without
changing the design. It is not part of the MIT-licensed code in this
repository.

The GIF has no licence text of its own. The C file that uses it,
`utils/logo.c`, credits the design to Angela Goodman, carries jwz's
permission notice (above) for its code, and asks that the logo not be
altered: "The logo is xscreensaver's identity". To use a different picture
in a local build without committing it, set `XS_LOGO` to the image file (see
`AGENTS.md`). The blob format is in `ximage-loader.h`.

Going well, with the port working on the host. The commit is still running its pre-commit hooks and hasn't landed yet. The files are staged and `HEAD` is unchanged.

**Working**
- Phosphor runs on the host: a green terminal session with the glow and fade, scale 3, a 25×15 grid, and text kept inside the round bezel's visible area.
- Upstream `phosphor.c` and `ansi-tty` are byte-identical copies, with notices rows added, including one for the font.
- The shim now has bitmap `XDrawLine`, `XGetImage`, `XPutImage` and `XCopyPlane`, plus `utf8_encode`/`utf8_decode` and `blurb.h`. The shim tests pass, 293 plus the new ones.
- The leak test passes: `leaks` reports 0 bytes after I fixed upstream's leaks in the wrapper.

**Caught along the way**
- A shared clip-mask change to `XFillRectangle` moved Bubbles' and Pacman's pinned frames. I made it Phosphor-only through the wrapper, and both are back to their pins.
- The full `test_hacks` run (5.5 minutes) now fails only on Phosphor's own hash. I've since pinned it from the frame I viewed, but I haven't re-run the suite with that pin.

**Next**
1. Let the commit land.
2. Run the mutation checks. The script is written and covers 14 shim mutants.
3. Re-run the full suite.
4. Build for the device and, since you've said I can, flash it and read fps and heap.

I haven't built for the device or measured speed yet. The risk is that every fading cell redraws each frame.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver/.claude/skills/device-run

# Flashing and measuring on the device

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- `pio run -e stopwatch`: build for the device. Add `-t upload` to flash.
  The device starts on a random hack; to pin one while examining it, prefix
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS='-DSTART_HACK=\"galaxy\"'` (a name from `g_hacks[]`,
  any case; an unknown name falls back to random and logs it). Rebuild without
  it afterwards, since the define sticks to the build. Unescaped quotes fail
  with "error: 'truchet' was not declared in this scope".
  It rotates to the next hack every 90 s (a button press restarts the count);
  `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5` shortens that for leak testing and `=0` turns it off. A
  pinned build still rotates, so add `=0` to measure one hack.
  The log prints `rotate -> <hack> heap= psram=` at each change. Combine flags
  in one `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` string.
  `-DBADGE_NAME=\"Rod\ B.\"` sets the name badge text (default "Rod" over
  "Begbie"; `\n` starts a new line). Check a
  flag reached the binary with
  `strings -a -n 3 .pio/build/stopwatch/firmware.elf | grep -c '^Rod B\.$'`:
  plain `strings` skips anything under 4 characters.
  `-DQR_URL=\"https://example.com\"` sets the QR overlay's target (default the
  LinkedIn profile). Check it reached the binary with
  `strings -a .pio/build/stopwatch/firmware.elf | grep -c 'example.com'`.
  In a worktree session the harness refuses backslash-escaped flag values and
  `$(cat file)`. Use `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS="'-DBADGE_NAME=\"Rod B.\"'
  '-DSTART_HACK=\"gears\"' -DROTATE_SECONDS=0"` with `.venv/bin/pio run -d
  firmware -e stopwatch -t upload` from the worktree root.
- Serial log: `.venv/bin/python -I tools/serial_capture.py <out-file>
  <seconds> [port]` reads `/dev/cu.usbmodem112401` at 115200 into a file and
  reopens the port when it goes away. Run it in the background with absolute
  paths, since background shells ignore `cd`. Lines to read:
  `run <hack> fps= step= push= sync= wait= rows=` (ms per frame in the hack,
  the push, the wait for the panel's TE edge before a synced push (only
  Unknown Pleasures; not counted in `push=`) and the wait; mean canvas rows
  sent per frame, 466 being a full push,
  though overlay redraws made while waiting can push it higher)
  and `switch -> <hack> press_waited=`. An empty capture, or "Device not
  configured", means the USB port went away and came back (a flash, a crash):
  reopen it in a loop. Opening the port resets the board
  (`rst:0x15 USB_UART_CHIP_RESET`, even with DTR/RTS held low): the overlay
  returns to nothing and a random hack starts. To measure one hack, flash a
  pinned build (`START_HACK` plus `ROTATE_SECONDS=0`), start the capture, then
  tap during it: the early windows are the baseline, the later ones have the
  overlay.
  `serial_capture.py` sets `dtr` and `rts` to False on an unopened
  `serial.Serial()` before `open()`, as any script of your own must: a reopen
  loop without that once parked the chip in its bootloader
  (`boot:0x3 ... waiting for download`, screen frozen). Recover, or reset just
  before a capture to log from boot (a hack's `fprintf(stderr)` reaches the
  log), with `.venv/bin/python .platformio/packages/tool-esptoolpy/esptool.py
  --chip esp32s3 --port /dev/cu.usbmodem112401 --after hard_reset read_mac`.
- Flash with `pio run -e stopwatch -t upload > file 2>&1`, never piped through
  `head`, and check for "Hash of data verified". The button steps backwards
  (Pyro, then Lightning, then Drift...). Work out how long a restart takes
  from the hack's cycle count times its frame time (Substrate: 10,000 cycles
  at about 160 ms is 27 minutes) and capture that long, with rotation off.
- `ad-flyingtoasters` force flags (add to `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS`):
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_ART=0|1` (0 is 1-bit, 1 is colour) and
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_DONENESS=0|1|2` (light, medium, dark) and
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_SCALE=1|2` (2 is the default, with 6 flyers; 1 is the
  original size, with 10); a number outside those is an `#error`. It logs
  `ad-flyingtoasters: <art>, doneness=<level>` to stderr at start.
- To see where a GL hack's frame goes, add `-DGL_PROFILE`: a `glprof` line
  follows each `run` line with time per stage (clear, list, vertex, shade,
  tri, fill, point, line; nested, so vertex includes tri and fill). Time left
  over is the hack's own code. To compare builds, `.venv/bin/python -I
  tools/ab_flash.py --hack Gears --seconds 60 --rounds 2 --out <dir>
  "a=-DGL_PROFILE" "b=-DGL_PROFILE -DFOO"` builds each variant pinned, flashes
  them in turn and tabulates the windows. It flashes: run it only with Rod's
  go-ahead. It builds each hack's variants from the working tree when that
  hack's turn starts, so leave `src/` and `tools/tinygl_patch.py` alone until
  the last hack has built. It compares flag variants of one tree: to A/B a
  change, put it behind a temporary `-D` switch (as `-DPUSH_NO_DISC` does).
  It takes one `--hack` per run: loop several from a scratchpad script run
  with `run_in_background`, and `touch` a done file at the end.
- `-DDCACHE_LINE32` keeps the SDK's 32-byte data-cache lines for every hack
  (the default is 64 bytes, see `device-display.md`), so it is the A side of an
  `ab_flash` comparison. `-DPSRAM_BENCH` boots into `diag/psram_bench.h`
  instead of the runner and prints cost per cache miss, sequential rates and a
  working-set sweep; `-DPSRAM_BENCH_VARIANT=0..3` picks the line size and
  prefetch setting.
- `esptool` reads of the 16 MB flash need `--baud 921600` (about 3.5 minutes)
  and show no progress when piped.
- The port name changes with the USB socket the board is plugged into
  (`/dev/cu.usbmodem112401` became `/dev/cu.usbmodem101` on 2026-10-14). When
  it is missing, find the board without touching it:
  `ioreg -p IOUSB -l -w0 | grep -E "\+-o|idVendor|idProduct|USB Product
  Name|USB Serial Number"` lists USB devices, and
  `ioreg -r -c IOSerialBSDClient -l | grep IOCalloutDevice` lists the serial
  ports. The StopWatch is the "USB JTAG/serial debug unit" from Espressif
  (`idVendor` 12346, `idProduct` 4097). Its USB serial number is its MAC:
  Rod's board is `28:84:85:43:B2:70`, so check that before flashing a port
  you have not used before. Pass `--upload-port <port>` to `pio run -t upload`
  and read the same port for the serial log, and leave `platformio.ini`'s
  `upload_port` alone. Still ask Rod before each flash. The auto-mode
  classifier refused a flash to an overridden port once: give Rod the command
  to run with `!`.
- Another session may be using the board. Before flashing, run `lsof
  /dev/cu.usbmodem112401`: a "multiple access on port" upload error was
  another session's serial capture, and esptool's connect resets the board
  under it. Ask Rod before flashing over someone else's run.
- PlatformIO cleans the build directory, image and all, when
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` changes: an `-t nobuild -t upload` with other flags
  finds no `firmware.bin`. To keep several images, give each its own
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_DIR` (the build scripts all use `$BUILD_DIR`).
- Read `push=` from a hack's second 5 s window on: the name overlay is stamped
  inside the push timing while it shows, so the first window reads high.
- `heap=` and `psram=` are the reading at the end of a window, not a minimum:
  a hack with a long pause and nothing held in it (Celtic's 5 s `*delay2`)
  reads idle in every window. Sample while it works, or read `rotate ->`.
- Report a hack's lowest `fps=` window as well as its mean. HexTrail's step
  grows over a 65 s cycle: mean 15.3, worst window 10.8, and Rod saw an earlier
  build sag under 10 fps before the rotation moved on. Capture a full cycle and
  say which build the board holds when you stop.
- A boot is deterministic (same hack, layout and windows), so to compare two
  builds flash them alternately and compare window by window; one reading in
  three captures was an unexplained outlier, so never trust a single pair.
- Leak-testing with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5`: internal heap falls about 26 KB
  during the first lap and then stays flat. Compare lap 2 with lap 3, not
  with lap 1. PSRAM should match exactly on every visit.
- To prove a device-only path the host cannot run (the ROM's `tinfl`), add a
  temporary `#ifdef` block after `printStats("boot")` in `main.cpp` that logs
  a checksum, compare it with one computed in Python, then `git checkout
  firmware/src/main.cpp` before pushing.

Rod, Phosphor is on the board now, pinned with rotation off, so it should be on screen.

**Please look at the screen and tell me:**
- Does the session read well on the round panel? The text is a canned boot log plus "Nobody asked for a glass terminal on a stopwatch." It starts at row 2 so the corners aren't clipped, and it loops about every 14 seconds.

- Does the phosphor glow and fade look right when the screen clears?

**Device numbers**
- **Speed:** about 17.6 fps while typing, paced by its own 50 ms delay, dipping to 11–12 fps in the 20–36 ms steps when the whole screen fades.
- **Memory:** free PSRAM and heap are flat across 90 s, with no stack canary or reboot lines. I haven't done a rotation soak yet.

**Status**
- The full host suite is running now, about 6 minutes.
- Everything is committed on `feature/ARS-58-phosphor` (3 commits).

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/.claude/skills/markdown

# GitHub Flavored Markdown Generation

**Version:** 1.2.1

Generate GFM that passes markdownlint validation with zero violations.

## Core Principles

### 1. Blank Lines Are Mandatory

- Before/after ALL lists (MD032)
- Before/after ALL headings except document start (MD022)
- Before/after ALL code blocks (MD031)
- Between ALL block-level elements

### 2. Consistency Required

- Use `-` for lists
- Use `#` for headings (ATX)
- Regular spaces only—never tabs/nbsp

### 3. Structure Matters

- Heading hierarchy: 1→2→3 (not 1→3)
- ONE H1 per document
- Files end with one newline
- Lines under 80 chars

### 4. Invisible Characters Matter

- Use ONLY regular spaces (U+0020)
- Never non-breaking spaces (U+00A0,  )
- Never tabs
- UTF-8 encoding

## Pre-Generation Checklist

- [ ] Where will lists/headings/code appear?
- [ ] Heading levels verified (1→2→3)?
- [ ] Using `-` for all lists?
- [ ] Code languages specified?
- [ ] Lines under 80 chars?
- [ ] Line breaks needed? (two trailing spaces)
- [ ] Using regular spaces only?
- [ ] URLs wrapped in `<>` or `[]`?
- [ ] Document starts with H1?
- [ ] Ordered lists use `1.` for all items?
- [ ] File ends with single newline?
- [ ] Tables use consistent spacing?

## Essential Rules

### Lists (MD032, MD004)

```markdown
Text before.

- Item one
- Item two

Text after.
```

### Headings (MD001, MD022)

```markdown
Text.

## Heading

Content.
```

### Code Blocks (MD031, MD040)

````markdown
Text.

```python
code()
```

Text.
````

**Nested Fences:** When showing markdown examples that contain code blocks,
use **one more backtick** than the deepest level:

- Three backticks (` ``` `): Regular code
- Four backticks (` ```` `): Markdown examples with code
- Five backticks (` ````` `): Nested markdown examples

`````markdown
````markdown
# Example

```bash
command
```

````
`````

### Line Length (MD013)

Break long lines at natural points. Use reference-style links for long URLs.

### URLs and Email (MD034)

Wrap bare URLs and emails:

```markdown
Wrong: https://example.com
Right: <https://example.com>
Right: [link](https://example.com)

Wrong: user@example.com
Right: <user@example.com>
```

### Document Structure (MD041)

Start with H1 (or front matter then H1):

```markdown
# Document Title

First paragraph.
```

### Ordered Lists (MD029)

Use `1.` for all items:

```markdown
1. First
1. Second
1. Third
```

### File Endings (MD047)

End with single newline:

```text
Last content line.
[single newline]
[EOF]
```

### Table Column Style (MD060)

Use consistent spacing in tables. Three styles:

**Compact (recommended):** `| cell |` - single space around content

```markdown
| Header 1 | Header 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Data | More data |
```

**Aligned:** Pipes vertically aligned with padding

**Tight:** `|cell|` - no spaces

Pick ONE style per document. Compact is preferred.

### Character Encoding

**Detection:** View → Render Whitespace in VS Code

**Fix:** Find `\u00A0` → Replace with space

**Critical for AI:** Two trailing spaces = intentional line breaks. Do NOT
remove them.

## Critical Error Patterns

### 1. List Without Blank Lines

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD032 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
Text:
- Item
Text.
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD032 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
Text:

- Item

Text.
```

### 2. Heading Without Blank Lines

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD022 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
Text.
## Head
Text.
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD022 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
Text.

## Head

Text.
```

### 3. Code Without Blanks/Language

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD031 MD040 -->

**Wrong:**

````markdown
Text:
```
code
```
Text.
````

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD031 MD040 -->

**Right:**

````markdown
Text:

```python
code
```

Text.
````

### 4. Inconsistent Markers

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD004 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
- Item
* Item
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD004 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
- Item
- Item
```

### 5. Skipping Levels

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD001 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
# Title

### Sub (skipped H2)
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD001 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
# Title

## Section

### Sub
```

## Post-Generation Validation

1. Lists have blank lines before/after
2. Headings have blank lines before/after
3. Code has blank lines before/after
4. Heading progression: 1→2→3→4
5. All lists use `-`
6. All code has language
7. Lines under 80 chars
8. Document starts with H1
9. URLs wrapped properly
10. Ordered lists use `1.`
11. File ends with one newline
12. Two trailing spaces used intentionally
13. Only regular spaces (no nbsp/tabs)
14. Tables use consistent column spacing

## Mental Model

Markdown is **blocks with mandatory spacing:**

```text
[Text Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Heading Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[List Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Code Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Text Block]
[EOF]
```

Every block transition = blank line required.

## Quick Patterns

**List:**

```markdown
text

- item

text
```

**Heading:**

```markdown
text

## Head

text
```

**Code:**

````markdown
text

```lang
code
```

text
````

**Nested:**

```markdown
- parent
  - child
- parent
```

**Ordered:**

```markdown
text

1. item
1. item

text
```

**Table:**

```markdown
text

| Header | Header |
| --- | --- |
| Cell | Cell |

text
```

## Common Languages

**Programming:** `python` `javascript` `java` `c` `cpp` `go` `rust` `ruby`
`php` `swift` `kotlin` `typescript`

**Shell:** `bash` `sh` `powershell` `cmd` `zsh`

**Markup:** `html` `css` `xml` `json` `yaml` `toml` `markdown`

**Database:** `sql` `postgresql` `mysql`

**Other:** `text` `diff` `log`

## Validation

```bash
markdownlint filename.md
```

Goal: Zero errors/warnings.

## Additional Resources

See bundled references:

- `references/complete-rules.md` - Full rule catalog
- `references/edge-cases.md` - Platform quirks
- `references/examples.md` - Detailed examples

## Remember

Most common: Missing blank lines around lists/headings/code.

**Two trailing spaces:** Intentional line breaks. Do NOT remove.

When in doubt:

1. Add blank lines before/after blocks
2. Use `-` for lists
3. Use `#` for headings
4. Specify code language
5. Increment headings by one
6. Use regular spaces only
7. Two trailing spaces = line break

p='tools/assessment_measured.md.in'
t=open(p).read()
k='| XJack | 7.8-15.8 | 0.1-13.8 ms | 0.3-15.0 ms | 46-130 ms | none measurable |\n'
assert k in t
t=t.replace(k,k+'| Phosphor (scale 3, canned session) | 11.0-17.8 (mean 16.0) | 0.6-35.7 ms | 0.3-5.1 ms | 50.2-55.4 ms | none measurable (free PSRAM 6,214,243 flat over 16 windows) |\n',1)
open(p,'w').write(t)

p='.claude/rules/hacks.md'
t=open(p).read()
t=t.rstrip('\n')+'''
- Phosphor (`phosphor_tty.c`, ARS-58) is an unmodified `phosphor.c` and
  `ansi-tty.c` behind a wrapper. Upstream reads a program on a pty
  (`xscreensaver-text`); the wrapper renames the `textclient_*` calls to a
  text source of its own, a canned boot log typed a character a frame that
  clears and loops (`kSession`; the shared `textclient.h` stays a NULL
  source, which XMatrix relies on). The text keeps to the columns the round
  panel shows on each row: the corners of the 25 by 15 grid are off the
  glass, and the first version's header sat in one. The wrapper overrides
  `*phosphorScale` to 3 (upstream's 6 is a 12 by 7 grid on 466 pixels) and
  `*cache: False` (a cache of every fade of every glyph is about 20 MB). The
  builtin 6 by 10 font is `images/gen/6x10font_png.h`, a blob made by
  `make_logo_blob.py --deflate` (1.3 KB). Upstream's glow is a fill through a
  clip mask, which `XFillRectangle` ignores, so the wrapper maps it to
  `xshim_fill_rect_clipped`: making the shared call honour the mask moved
  Bubbles' and Pacman's pinned frames, and without any such fill every
  letter was a solid cell (`test_phosphor_draws_letters_not_solid_cells`).
  Upstream's free leaves the tty grid, the Xft handle, three of its four
  glyph sets' structs and the first font pass's three GCs (it runs the pass
  twice and overwrites its GCs); the wrapper frees all of them. On the board:
  11.0-17.8 fps (mean 16.0), paced by its own 50 ms delay while typing (step
  0.6-2 ms) and 20-36 ms when the screen clears and every cell fades at once.
  `ansi-tty.c` writes to `stderr` only with `debug_p` set, and on the board
  that expands to `_impure_ptr`, which the toolchain lacks: `blurb.h` gives
  the file a null `stderr` there.
'''
open(p,'w').write(t)

p='.claude/rules/x11shim.md'
t=open(p).read()
t=t.rstrip('\n')+'''
- Added for Phosphor (ARS-58), each test-first: `XDrawLine` on a bitmap (thin
  lines walk the longer axis and round halves up; wide lines are a rectangle
  plus 16-sided discs for a round cap, centred as `stroke.c` does), `XGetImage`
  of a bitmap (an `XYPixmap` request gives a 1-bit image), `XPutImage` onto a
  bitmap, `XCopyPlane` between bitmaps (set bits take the GC's foreground and
  clear bits its background, the low bit of each; it honours the clip mask),
  `utf8_encode` and `utf8_decode`, and a `blurb.h`. `XFillRectangle` still
  ignores a clip mask: `xshim_fill_rect_clipped` (`pixmap.h`) is the clipped
  fill, and only Phosphor's wrapper calls it, since making the shared call
  honour the mask moved Bubbles' and Pacman's pinned frames.
'''
open(p,'w').write(t)
EOF
markdownlint .claude/rules/hacks.md .claude/rules/x11shim.md; echo rc=$?; git diff --stat | tail -4

content.text:
Phosphor is ported and running on the board, pinned with rotation off, so it should be on screen now. I'd like you to look at it before I open the PR.

**Please check:**
- Is the text legible on the round panel? It is a canned boot log, "Nobody asked for a glass terminal on a stopwatch.", loops about every 14 s, and is kept inside the circle's visible columns.
- Is scale 3 (a 25×15 grid) the right size? Scale 4 gives bigger letters on a 19×11 grid.
- Does the phosphor glow and fade look right when the screen clears?

**Where it stands**
- **Host:** the full native suite passes (899 of 899) and the Python tests pass (652 passed, 1 skipped). `check_notices` is clean.
- **Device:** 11.0–17.8 fps (mean 16.0), paced by its own 50 ms delay. The dips to 11–12 fps come from 20–36 ms steps when the whole screen fades after a clear. Free PSRAM was flat over 16 windows, with no stack canary or reboot lines. I haven't done a rotation soak yet.
- **Tests:** I mutation-checked the new shim code (all killed, after adding one test for a survivor). I did the same for the wrapper's clipped fill and its leak fixes (all killed).
