content.text:
I think it enters the US public domain on 1 January 2030. That is my answer from earlier, in case it got lost behind the tool output.

- **US:** I believe the poem was first published in 1934, and US copyright runs 95 years from publication, which gives 2030. That assumes copyright was properly renewed.
- **Life plus 70 (UK, EU and similar):** Williams died in 1963, so those countries would be 1 January 2034.
- **Confidence:** I'm not certain of the first-publication year or the renewal history, and this isn't legal advice. I'd check before relying on it, which is why I'm keeping to pre-1931 poems.

The full `test_hacks` run is still going in the background.

t=open(p).read()

new='''- Phosphor (`phosphor_tty.c`, ARS-58) is an unmodified `phosphor.c` and
  `ansi-tty.c` behind a wrapper. Upstream reads a program on a pty
  (`xscreensaver-text`); the wrapper renames the `textclient_*` calls to a
  text source of its own (`phosphor_text.h`, tested directly): it `cat`s one
  of seven public-domain poems, picked at random and never the one just shown,
  typed a character a frame. The shared `textclient.h` stays a NULL source,
  which XMatrix relies on. `firmware/assets/phosphor-poems.txt` is the source
  text; `tools/make_phosphor_poems.py` word-wraps it to 18 columns (4 in, the
  columns the round panel shows on rows 2 to 13: the corners of the 25 by 15
  grid are off the glass) and pages it into `phosphor_poems.h`. Nothing
  scrolls: Phosphor leaves a ghost of every character a scroll moves, which
  read as noise under the new text, so a page ends with `--More--`, a pause
  byte (`\\001`) and then a clear. Only poems published before 1931 go in
  (`THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`); the Raven, Ozymandias, two Frost poems, Williams's
  Red Wheelbarrow (1923), Blake and Dickinson are in. The wrapper overrides
  `*phosphorScale` to 3 (upstream's 6 is a 12 by 7 grid on 466 pixels) and
  `*cache: False` (a cache of every fade of every glyph is about 20 MB). The
  builtin 6 by 10 font is `images/gen/6x10font_png.h`, a blob made by
  `make_logo_blob.py --deflate` (1.3 KB). Upstream's glow is a fill through a
  clip mask, which `XFillRectangle` ignores, so the wrapper maps it to
  `xshim_fill_rect_clipped`: making the shared call honour the mask moved
  Bubbles' and Pacman's pinned frames, and without any such fill every
  letter was a solid cell (`test_phosphor_draws_letters_not_solid_cells`).
  Upstream's free leaves the tty grid, the Xft handle, three of its four
  glyph sets' structs and the first font pass's three GCs (it runs the pass
  twice and overwrites its GCs); the wrapper frees all of them. On the board:
  13.0-17.6 fps (mean 16.2), paced by its own 50 ms delay while typing (step
  1.4-2 ms) and up to 22 ms when a page clears and every cell fades at once.
  `ansi-tty.c` writes to `stderr` only with `debug_p` set, and on the board
  that expands to `_impure_ptr`, which the toolchain lacks: `blurb.h` gives
  the file a null `stderr` there. `pio test` and `pio run -e stopwatch` must
  not overlap: the test run clears shared build state and the flash fails
  with a missing `firmware.elf`.
'''
t=t[:a]+new
open(p,'w').write(t)
EOF

The poem version is working and is on the board now, pinned to Phosphor with rotation off. Each loop it picks one of seven poems and never repeats the last one.

**The poems**
- All seven were published before 1931, so they're public domain in the US: The Raven (first stanza), Ozymandias, Fire and Ice, Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening, The Red Wheelbarrow, The Tyger and Hope is the thing with feathers.
- The texts come from Wikisource's transcriptions of the first printings, and `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` lists them.
- I used The Red Wheelbarrow instead of This Is Just To Say, because the latter is still in copyright. Williams's 1923 poem has been public domain since 2019.
- Original spellings are kept ("desart" in Ozymandias, "sieze" in The Tyger).

**What you'll see**
- Each loop starts with `> cat raven`, then the poem types out a character at a time.
- A long poem is shown in pages, ending in `--More--`, then the screen clears and the next page types. Scrolling smeared ghosts of the old text under the new, so I used pages instead.
- Lines are word-wrapped to 18 columns and kept to the rows and columns the round panel shows, so nothing sits in the clipped corners.

**Device numbers (22 windows over 120 s)**
- 13.0–17.6 fps (mean 16.2), paced by its own 50 ms delay.
- Steps are 1.4–22 ms. Free PSRAM is flat, with no stack canary or reboot lines.
- That's the same speed as before, and the same glow you approved.

**Tests**
- The full native suite passes: 909 of 909. The Python tests for the poem generator pass.
- I mutation-checked the poem selection, the page and pause handling, and the generator, and all mutants are killed. One extra test came out of that: the first run left three survivors, all about what happens when a page or poem ends. I moved that logic into `phosphor_text.h` so it can be tested directly, and all three are now killed.
- Everything is committed on `feature/ARS-58-phosphor` (6 commits, latest 0fdeb9a), not yet pushed.

**Your call:** please look at the screen and check the pages read well, especially the long ones (Ozymandias is 7 pages, Woods is 6). If it's good I'll:
1. Open the draft PR via `deliver-branch`, with ARS-58 moved to In Review.
2. Re-flash a plain rotating build, so the board isn't left pinned to Phosphor.

XIII.

 

 

I wandered lonely as a Cloud

That floats on high o'er Vales and Hills,

When all at once I saw a crowd,

A host of golden Daffodils;

Beside the Lake, beneath the trees,

Fluttering and dancing in the breeze.

Continuous as the stars that shine

And twinkle on the milky way,

They stretched in never-ending line

Along the margin of a bay:

Ten thousand saw I at a glance,

Tossing their heads in sprightly dance.

The waves beside them danced, but they

Out-did the sparkling waves in glee:—

A Poet could not but be gay

In such a jocund company:

I gazed—and gazed—but little thought

What wealth the shew to me had brought:

  For oft when on my couch I lie

In vacant or in pensive mood,

They flash upon that inward eye

Which is the bliss of solitude,

And then my heart with pleasure fills,

And dances with the Daffodils.

=== Maud, and other poems/The Charge of the Light Brigade (1614)
GE OF THE LIGHT BRIGADE.

1.

Half a league, half a league,

Half a league onward,

All in the valley of Death

Rode the six hundred.

"Charge," was the captain's cry;

Their's not to reason why,

Their's not to make reply,

Their's but to do and die,

Into the valley of Death

Rode the six hundred.

  
2.

Cannon to right of them,

Cannon to left of them,

Cannon in front of them

Volley'd and thunder'd;

Storm'd at with shot and shell,

Boldly they rode and well;

Into the jaws of Death,

Into the mouth of Hell,

Rode the six hundred.

3.

Flash'd all their sabres bare,

Flash'd all at once in air,

Sabring the gunners there,

Charging an army, while

All the world wonder'd:

Plunged in the battery-smoke
  Fiercely the line they broke;

Strong was the sabre-stroke;

Making an army reel

Shaken and sunder'd.

Then they rode back, but not,

Not the six hundred.

4.

Cannon to right of them,

Cannon to left of them,

Cannon behind them

Volley'd and thunder'd;

Storm'd at with shot and shell,

They that had struck so well

Rode thro' the jaws of Death,

Half a league back again,

Up from the mouth of Hell,

All that was left of them,

Left of six hundred.

  
5.

Honour the brave and bold!

Long shall the tale be told,

Yea, when our babes are old—

How they rode onward.

THE END.

=== The Poetical Works of Robert Burns/To a Mouse, on turning her up in her nest, with the plough (1990)
 THE PLOUGH, NOVEMBER, 1785.

Wee, sleekit, cow'rin, tim'rous beastie, 
O, what a panic's in thy breastie!
Thou need na start awa sae hasty,
Wi' bickering brattle!
I wad be laith to rin an' chase thee,
Wi' murd'ring pattle!

I'm truly sorry man's dominion
Has broken Nature's social union,
An' justifies that ill opinion,
Which makes thee startle,
At me, thy poor, earth-born companion,
An' fellow-mortal!

I doubt na, whiles, but thou may thieve;
What then? poor beastie, thou maun live!
A daimen-icker in a thrave
'S a sma' request:
I'll get a blessin wi' the lave,
And never miss't!

Thy wee bit housie, too, in ruin!
Its silly wa's the win's are strewin!
An' naething, now, to big a new ane,
O' foggage green;
An' bleak December's winds ensuin,
Baith snell an' keen!

  Thou saw the fields laid bare an' waste,
An' weary winter comin fast,
An' cozie here, beneath the blast,
Thou thought to dwell,
Till crash! the cruel coulter past,
Out thro' thy cell.

That wee bit heap o' leaves an' stibble,
Has cost thee mony a weary nibble!
Now thou's turn'd out, for a' thy trouble,
But house or hald,
To thole the winter's sleety dribble,
An' cranreuch cauld!

But, Mousie, thou art no thy lane,
In proving foresight may be vain:
The best laid schemes o' mice an' men
Gang aft a-gley,
An' lea'e us nought but grief an' pain,
For promis'd joy.

Still thou art blest, compar'd wi' me!
The present only toucheth thee:
But, Och! I backward cast my e'e
On prospects drear!
An' forward, tho' I canna see,
I guess an' fear!

Half a league, half a league,
 Half a league onward,
All in the valley of Death
 Rode the six hundred.
  "Forward, the Light Brigade!
Charge for the guns!" he said:
Into the valley of Death
 Rode the six hundred.

"Forward, the Light Brigade!"
Was there a man dismay'd?
Not tho' the soldier knew
 Some one had blunder'd:
Theirs not to make reply,
Theirs not to reason why,
Theirs but to do and die:
Into the valley of Death
 Rode the six hundred.

Cannon to right of them,
Cannon to left of them,
Cannon in front of them
 Volley'd and thunder'd;
Storm'd at with shot and shell,
Boldly they rode and well,
Into the jaws of Death,
Into the mouth of Hell
 Rode the six hundred.

Flash'd all their sabers bare,
Flash'd as they turn'd in air
Sab'ring the gunners there,
Charging an army, while
 All the world wonder'd:
Plunged in the battery-smoke
Right thro' the line they broke;
  Cossack and Russian
Reel'd from the saber-stroke
 Shatter'd and sunder'd.
Then they rode back, but not
 Not the six hundred.

Cannon to right of them,
Cannon to left of them,
Cannon behind them
 Volleyed and thundered:
Stormed at with shot and shell,
While horse and hero fell,
They that had fought so well
Came through the jaws of death
Back from the mouth of hell,
All that was left of them—
 Left of six hundred.

When can their glory fade?
Oh, the wild charge they made!
 All the world wondered.
Honour the charge they made!
Honour the Light Brigade—
 Noble six hundred!
Alfred Tennyson.

"""Turn firmware/assets/phosphor-poems.txt into the C header Phosphor's text
source reads.

Each poem becomes one string of terminal output: clear the screen, type a
`cat` command, then the poem word-wrapped to fit the part of the round panel
that shows (see the table below). A poem that does not fit is paged: the page
ends with `--More--` and a pause byte, and the next page clears the screen.
Phosphor leaves a ghost of every character a scroll moves, which reads as
noise under the new text, so nothing scrolls.

Run with: uv run tools/make_phosphor_poems.py
"""

import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
SOURCE = ROOT / "firmware" / "assets" / "phosphor-poems.txt"
OUTPUT = ROOT / "firmware" / "src" / "hacks" / "phosphor_poems.h"

# At scale 3 the grid is 25 by 15 cells, and the circle shows columns 4 to 21
# on rows 2 to 13 (rows 0, 1 and 14 are mostly off the glass).
INDENT = 4
WIDTH = 18
HANGING = 2
FIRST_ROW = 2
LAST_ROW = 13
# The command takes row 2 and a gap row 3, so a page has rows 4 to 13: ten.
PAGE_ROWS = LAST_ROW - (FIRST_ROW + 2) + 1
MORE = "--More--"
# The last page ends with a blank row, the byline and a prompt row.
TAIL_ROWS = 3
# The byte the text source waits on; the terminal never sees it.
PAUSE = "\x01"

CLEAR = "\x1b[2J\x1b[H"


def wrap(line: str) -> list[str]:
    """Greedy word wrap: the first piece WIDTH wide, later ones HANGING
    narrower and indented by it. A word longer than the room is an error."""
    pieces: list[str] = []
    current = ""

    def room() -> int:
        return WIDTH if not pieces else WIDTH - HANGING

    for word in line.split():
        if current and len(current) + 1 + len(word) <= room():
            current += " " + word
            continue
        if current:
            pieces.append(current)
        if len(word) > room():
            raise ValueError(f"{word!r} is wider than {room()} columns")
        current = word
    pieces.append(current)
    return [pieces[0]] + [" " * HANGING + p for p in pieces[1:]]


def parse(text: str) -> list[tuple[str, str, list[str]]]:
    """(file name, byline, lines) for each poem; a blank line is kept."""
    poems: list[tuple[str, str, list[str]]] = []
    for raw in text.splitlines():
        if raw.startswith("#"):
            continue
        if raw.startswith("== "):
            name, _, byline = raw[3:].partition("|")
            poems.append((name.strip(), byline.strip(), []))
        elif poems:
            poems[-1][2].append(raw.rstrip())
        elif raw.strip():
            raise ValueError(f"text before the first poem: {raw!r}")
    for name, byline, lines in poems:
        while lines and not lines[-1]:
            lines.pop()
        if not name or not byline or not lines:
            raise ValueError(f"poem {name!r} needs a name, a byline and lines")
        for line in [name, byline, *lines]:
            if not line.isascii():
                raise ValueError(
                    f"{line!r} is not ASCII: the font has no glyphs for it"
                )
    return poems


def paginate(groups: list[list[str]]) -> list[list[str]]:
    """Rows of each page. A group (one verse line, wrapped) is never split. A
    page that is not the last keeps a row for --More--, and the last keeps rows
    for a blank, the byline and the prompt. Blank rows at a page's edges go."""
    final_room = PAGE_ROWS - TAIL_ROWS
    pages: list[list[str]] = []
    i = 0
    while True:
        while i < len(groups) and groups[i] == [""]:
            i += 1
        rest = groups[i:]
        while rest and rest[-1] == [""]:
            rest.pop()
        if sum(len(g) for g in rest) <= final_room:
            pages.append([row for g in rest for row in g])
            return pages
        page: list[str] = []
        last = i + len(rest) - 1  # the last page keeps at least the last group
        while i < last and len(page) + len(groups[i]) <= PAGE_ROWS - 1:
            page += groups[i]
            i += 1
        if not page:
            raise ValueError(f"{groups[i]!r} does not fit on a page")
        while page and page[-1] == "":
            page.pop()
        pages.append(page)


def render(name: str, byline: str, lines: list[str]) -> str:
    """The terminal output for one poem."""
    groups = [wrap(line) if line else [""] for line in lines]
    pages = paginate(groups)
    out = []
    for number, rows in enumerate(pages):
        out.append(CLEAR + "\r\n" * FIRST_ROW)
        out.append(" " * INDENT + f"> cat {name}\r\n\r\n")
        if number + 1 < len(pages):
            rows = [*rows, MORE]
        else:
            rows = [*rows, "", f"-- {byline}", "> _"]
        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            out.append(" " * INDENT + row if row else "")
            if i + 1 < len(rows):
                out.append("\r\n")
        if number + 1 < len(pages):
            out.append(PAUSE)
    return "".join(out)


def c_string(text: str) -> str:
    """A C string literal, split after each newline so the lines stay short."""
    chunks = text.split("\n")
    pieces = []
    for i, chunk in enumerate(chunks):
        piece = chunk + ("\n" if i + 1 < len(chunks) else "")
        if not piece:
            continue
        escaped = (
            piece.replace("\\", "\\\\")
            .replace('"', '\\"')
            .replace("\x1b", "\\033")
            .replace("\r", "\\r")
            .replace("\n", "\\n")
        )
        pieces.append(f'    "{escaped}"')
    return "\n".join(pieces)


def header(text: str) -> str:
    poems = parse(text)
    body = []
    for name, byline, lines in poems:
        body.append(f"    /* {name} */\n{c_string(render(name, byline, lines))},")
    entries = "\n".join(body)
    return (
        "/* Generated by tools/make_phosphor_poems.py from "
        "firmware/assets/phosphor-poems.txt; do not edit. */\n"
        "#ifndef PHOSPHOR_POEMS_H\n"
        "#define PHOSPHOR_POEMS_H\n\n"
        "static const char *const kPoems[] = {\n"
        f"{entries}\n"
        "};\n\n"
        "#define POEM_COUNT ((int)(sizeof kPoems / sizeof kPoems[0]))\n\n"
        "#endif\n"
    )


def main(argv: list[str]) -> int:
    text = header(SOURCE.read_text())
    if not OUTPUT.exists() or OUTPUT.read_text() != text:
        OUTPUT.write_text(text)
    print(f"{OUTPUT.relative_to(ROOT)}: {len(parse(SOURCE.read_text()))} poems")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv[1:]))

# Scorer and speed-prediction gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- `score_hacks.py` rates effort by call sites, not loop trips: Flame (all
  `double` maths) is rated S but runs at 2-7 fps, and Braid was rated S and
  runs at 3-9 fps. The Speed column runs the hack on the host instead and ranks
  the device step well (Spearman about 0.9 over the 29 hacks it was fitted to,
  and four more ported since fell where predicted), but a low band does not
  clear a hack that does software `double` maths: the device ran 60-1,500
  times the host time, most for the double-bound ones. It says nothing about
  memory: Celtic as copied held about 300 KB of the 325 KB of free heap and
  ran at 1.2 fps (it is registered again after issue #37, see `hacks.md`). A
  failed port that has its source and a measured row (Hypnowheel, Boing)
  still counts in `speed_backtest.py`, probed standalone. Measure on the
  device, and read
  `docs/speed-backtest.md` before trusting a band. A hack with gaps (M and
  above) cannot be built, so it has no Speed.
- A `failed_ports.txt` name is the scorer's: the source file's stem
  (`companion` for Companion Cube), as the assessment's rows spell it. Check
  the cross appears after regenerating.
- `score_hacks.py --no-probe` also blanks the Speed column of the generated
  assessment ("high (2 ms)" becomes "-"): commit the output of a full run. The
  backtest reads a measured row only when its name is the bare hack name
  (`| Deluxe |`); a row with a note in brackets is skipped, so put the build
  that is registered in the bare row.
- `score_hacks.py` counts a hack as ported if `&<name>_hack` appears anywhere
  in the text of `g_hacks[]`, `#ifdef` or not, and then refuses one that
  `failed_ports.txt` also lists. A probe-only entry (Hypnowheel's
  `HYPNOWHEEL_PROBE`) goes through a macro defined above the array.
- `speed_backtest.py` probes a dropped (shelved) hack standalone. A GL one
  (its source has `USE_GL`: Hypnowheel) is built with the GL layer through
  `gl_budget.measure`, which also converts the `images/gen/<n>_png.h` textures
  it includes. One that still cannot be built (BlockTube needs `glFogi`, which
  the GL layer lacks) is left out with a `note:` on stderr, so read the run's
  output for notes. The scorer also lists calls inside code that is never
  compiled (`XCreateBitmapFromData` in Cynosure's `DO_STIPPLE` block) as gaps.
- `score_hacks.py` skips the names in `OWN_HACKS` (our own hacks with no
  xscreensaver source, now `ad_flyingtoasters`) and still reports any other
  registry name it cannot scan as a typo. `speed_backtest.py` runs on the host
  only the registered hacks that have a device-measured row, so a `dump` build
  without the After Dark disk (which lacks the toasters) still works.
- `probe_hacks.MEASURED_ROW` takes only a number range in the fps cell: a
  row like `| HexTrail | 10.8-50.6, mean 15.3 |` is skipped, so the assessment
  shows `-` for its step and the backtest leaves it out. Put the mean in the
  prose.
- A call to an undeclared shim function also shows up as a gap named
  `error: incompatible integer to pointer conversion ...` (the implicit `int`
  return). It is noise beside the real gap (Barcode's `utf8_to_latin1`), but it
  counts towards the band.

# Scorer and speed-prediction gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- `score_hacks.py` rates effort by call sites, not loop trips: Flame (all
  `double` maths) is rated S but runs at 2-7 fps, and Braid was rated S and
  runs at 3-9 fps. The Speed column runs the hack on the host instead and ranks
  the device step well (Spearman about 0.9 over the 29 hacks it was fitted to,
  and four more ported since fell where predicted), but a low band does not
  clear a hack that does software `double` maths: the device ran 60-1,500
  times the host time, most for the double-bound ones. It says nothing about
  memory: Celtic as copied held about 300 KB of the 325 KB of free heap and
  ran at 1.2 fps (it is registered again after issue #37, see `hacks.md`). A
  failed port that has its source and a measured row (Hypnowheel, Boing)
  still counts in `speed_backtest.py`, probed standalone. Measure on the
  device, and read
  `docs/speed-backtest.md` before trusting a band. A hack with gaps (M and
  above) cannot be built, so it has no Speed.
- A `failed_ports.txt` name is the scorer's: the source file's stem
  (`companion` for Companion Cube), as the assessment's rows spell it. Check
  the cross appears after regenerating.
- `score_hacks.py --no-probe` also blanks the Speed column of the generated
  assessment ("high (2 ms)" becomes "-"): commit the output of a full run. The
  backtest reads a measured row only when its name is the bare hack name
  (`| Deluxe |`); a row with a note in brackets is skipped, so put the build
  that is registered in the bare row.
- `score_hacks.py` counts a hack as ported if `&<name>_hack` appears anywhere
  in the text of `g_hacks[]`, `#ifdef` or not, and then refuses one that
  `failed_ports.txt` also lists. A probe-only entry (Hypnowheel's
  `HYPNOWHEEL_PROBE`) goes through a macro defined above the array.
- `speed_backtest.py` probes a dropped (shelved) hack standalone. A GL one
  (its source has `USE_GL`: Hypnowheel) is built with the GL layer through
  `gl_budget.measure`, which also converts the `images/gen/<n>_png.h` textures
  it includes. One that still cannot be built (BlockTube needs `glFogi`, which
  the GL layer lacks) is left out with a `note:` on stderr, so read the run's
  output for notes. The scorer also lists calls inside code that is never
  compiled (`XCreateBitmapFromData` in Cynosure's `DO_STIPPLE` block) as gaps.
- `score_hacks.py` skips the names in `OWN_HACKS` (our own hacks with no
  xscreensaver source, now `ad_flyingtoasters`) and still reports any other
  registry name it cannot scan as a typo. `speed_backtest.py` runs on the host

== daffodils | Wordsworth, 1815
I wandered lonely as a Cloud
That floats on high o'er Vales and Hills,
When all at once I saw a crowd,
A host of golden Daffodils;
Beside the Lake, beneath the trees,
Fluttering and dancing in the breeze.

Continuous as the stars that shine
And twinkle on the milky way,
They stretched in never-ending line
Along the margin of a bay:
Ten thousand saw I at a glance,
Tossing their heads in sprightly dance.

The waves beside them danced, but they
Out-did the sparkling waves in glee:--
A Poet could not but be gay
In such a jocund company:
I gazed--and gazed--but little thought
What wealth the shew to me had brought:

For oft when on my couch I lie
In vacant or in pensive mood,
They flash upon that inward eye
Which is the bliss of solitude,
And then my heart with pleasure fills,
And dances with the Daffodils.

== charge | Tennyson, 1854
Half a league, half a league,
Half a league onward,
All in the valley of Death
Rode the six hundred.
"Forward, the Light Brigade!
Charge for the guns!" he said:
Into the valley of Death
Rode the six hundred.

"Forward, the Light Brigade!"
Was there a man dismay'd?
Not tho' the soldier knew
Some one had blunder'd:
Theirs not to make reply,
Theirs not to reason why,
Theirs but to do and die:
Into the valley of Death
Rode the six hundred.

Cannon to right of them,
Cannon to left of them,
Cannon in front of them
Volley'd and thunder'd;
Storm'd at with shot and shell,
Boldly they rode and well,
Into the jaws of Death,
Into the mouth of Hell
Rode the six hundred.

Flash'd all their sabers bare,
Flash'd as they turn'd in air
Sab'ring the gunners there,
Charging an army, while
All the world wonder'd:
Plunged in the battery-smoke
Right thro' the line they broke;
Cossack and Russian
Reel'd from the saber-stroke
Shatter'd and sunder'd.
Then they rode back, but not
Not the six hundred.

Cannon to right of them,
Cannon to left of them,
Cannon behind them
Volleyed and thundered:
Stormed at with shot and shell,
While horse and hero fell,
They that had fought so well
Came through the jaws of death
Back from the mouth of hell,
All that was left of them--
Left of six hundred.

content.text:
Scrolling costs noticeably more than paging, so here is the comparison, with the scrolling build now on the board for you to watch.

| | Paged | Scrolling |
| --- | --- | --- |
| fps | 13.0–17.6, mean 16.2 | 10.0–17.6, mean 13.6 |
| Step | 1.4–22 ms | 1.6–44.8 ms (mean 21.8) |
| Push | 0.5–3.2 ms | 0.6–9.7 ms (mean 4.6) |
| Rows pushed per frame | about 48 | 30–281 (mean 150) |

- **Why it costs more:** every scroll moves the whole text block up a row, so every cell is redrawn at once and many rows get pushed. Paging only redraws at a clear.
- **What stays the same:** free PSRAM is flat, and there are no canary or reboot lines.
- **Dips:** scrolling drops to 10.0–11.8 fps in many windows. That's the worst case I've seen for this hack, and it's what you'd notice by eye as steadier or choppier typing.
- **Looks:** you'll also see the ghost afterimages on every scroll that made me switch to paging. If you like that smeared-phosphor look, that's a point for scrolling.

**New poems**
- **Added:** I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud (Wordsworth, 1815 text), The Charge of the Light Brigade (Tennyson) and To a Mouse (Burns). That makes ten.
- **Charge text:** I used the standard six-stanza version, from the 1904 *Poems That Every Child Should Know* anthology on Wikisource.
- **Length:** Charge and Mouse are long: about 2,700 characters each, or around two minutes of typing. In paged mode that is 14–15 pages.
- **Byline:** bylines now wrap, so "-- Wordsworth, 1815" doesn't run past the circle.

**How I built it**
- Both layouts are generated and committed: `phosphor_poems.h` for pages and `phosphor_poems_scroll.h` for scrolling.
- `-DPHOSPHOR_SCROLL` picks the scrolling one, and paged is still the default.
- The generator tests pass (21).

**Still running:** the `test_hacks` re-pin. With ten poems, seed 1 may now pick a different poem, so the pinned hash will change. I haven't committed this round yet.

**Your call:** which do you want as the default, paged (smoother) or scrolling (more authentic phosphor, but down to 10 fps at times)? Once you've said, I'll commit with the right default, add the notices entries for the three new poems, and open the PR.

lastPrompt: Lovely.  Scrolling should be the default.  One last question: Would tehre be a way to make the cursor blink?  That's the only thing I'm missing in this

content.text:
Yes, the cursor can blink, and it's being built and checked now.

- **Cause:** upstream blinks the cursor with Xt timers, and the shim's timers never fire because the board has no event loop.
- **Fix:** the wrapper gets a four-slot timer queue of its own (`phosphor_timers.h`). It catches upstream's two timer calls and fires whatever is due once per draw. Nothing shared changes, so no other hack is affected.
- **Behaviour:** upstream's timing is about two-thirds of a second on and a third off, restarting whenever the cursor moves.
- **Scrolling default:** scrolling is now the default, and `-DPHOSPHOR_PAGED` gives the paged layout.

I'm running the blink test and its mutation checks in the background. The test uses a clock I move by hand and checks that, once the shortest poem has finished typing, the screen alternates between exactly two pictures, cursor on and cursor off. That's about 11 mutants and a few minutes. After that I'll re-pin the hash, run the full suite, flash the result and capture it so you can see it blink.

  Williams, 1923.

  (1794), with its original spelling.

  Emily Dickinson* (Little, Brown).
- "I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud", William Wordsworth, from *Poems* (1815),
  with its original capitals and spelling.
- "The Charge of the Light Brigade", Alfred, Lord Tennyson, first published in
  1854, from the revised text in *Poems That Every Child Should Know* (1904).
- "To a Mouse", Robert Burns, 1785, from *The Poetical Works of Robert Burns*,
  in Scots.

content.text: Kipling's "If—" was published in 1910, and Kipling died in 1936, so it is public domain. Fetching a transcription now. Adding it changes the poem count, so the pin run in progress will need repeating, and I'll fold it into one final pass.

```javascript
async function api(q){const r=await fetch("https://en.wikisource.org/w/api.php?format=json&"+q);return r.json();}
const s=await api("action=query&list=search&srlimit=6&srsearch="+encodeURIComponent("Kipling If you can keep your head when all about you"));
console.log(s.query.search.map(x=>x.title).join(" | "));
async function html(p){const r=await fetch("https://en.wikisource.org/w/api.php?format=json&action=parse&redirects=1&prop=text&page="+encodeURIComponent(p));const j=await r.json();return j.parse?j.parse.text["*"]:"MISSING";}
function plain(h){return h.replace(/<style[\s\S]*?<\/style>/g,"").replace(/<sup[\s\S]*?<\/sup>/g,"").replace(/<br\s*\/?>/g,"\n").replace(/<\/(p|div|li|dd|dt)>/g,"\n").replace(/<[^>]+>/g,"").replace(/ | |​| /g," ").replace(/&/g,"&").replace(/"/g,'"').replace(/'/g,"'").replace(/\n{3,}/g,"\n\n").trim();}
for (const p of ["Rewards and Fairies/If—","If—"]) { const t=plain(await html(p)); const i=t.search(/If you can keep your head/); console.log("=== "+p+" ("+t.length+")\n"+(i>=0?t.slice(Math.max(0,i-60),i+1700):t.slice(0,500))); }
```

8Rewards and Fairies — If—Rudyard Kipling

 
IF—

If you can keep your head when all about you

Are losing theirs and blaming it on you;

If you can trust yourself when all men doubt you,

But make allowance for their doubting too:

If you can wait and not be tired by waiting,

Or being lied about, don't deal in lies,

Or being hated don't give way to hating,

And yet don't look too good, nor talk too wise;

If you can dream—and not make dreams your master;

If you can think—and not make thoughts your aim,

If you can meet with Triumph and Disaster

And treat those two impostors just the same:

If you can bear to hear the truth you've spoken

Twisted by knaves to make a trap for fools,

Or watch the things you gave your life to, broken,

And stoop and build 'em up with worn-out tools;

If you can make one heap of all your winnings

And risk it on one turn of pitch-and-toss,

And lose, and start again at your beginnings

And never breathe a word about your loss:
  If you can force your heart and nerve and sinew

To serve your turn long after they are gone,

And so hold on when there is nothing in you

Except the Will which says to them: 'Hold on!'

If you can talk with crowds and keep your virtue,

Or walk with Kings—nor lose the common touch,

If neither foes nor loving friends can hurt you,

If all men count with you, but none too much:

If you can fill the unforgiving minute

With sixty seconds' worth of distance run,

Yours is the Earth and everything that's in it,

And—which is more—you'll be a Man, my son!
